#10500. How Developers Can Improve Their Learning and Productivity With AI

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how developers learn, write code, and manage their daily work. Tasks that once required hours of searching, testing, and manual effort can now be completed with help from AI. Developers can use it to understand complex programming concepts, find coding errors, learn new technologies, and complete repetitive tasks.

However, AI is not only useful for writing code faster. It can also help developers improve their technical knowledge, solve problems, and build better learning habits. When used correctly, it can become a useful assistant throughout the software development process.

The key is to understand where AI can help and where human skills are still needed. Here are several practical ways developers can use AI to improve their learning and productivity.

Learning a new programming language or understanding a difficult concept can take time. Developers often need to read long explanations, watch tutorials, and test different examples before they understand how something works.

AI can make this process easier by explaining technical concepts in simple language. Instead of searching through several websites, developers can ask direct questions and receive explanations based on their current knowledge.

For example, a developer learning JavaScript can ask AI to explain promises, callbacks, or asynchronous functions. It can break these topics into smaller parts and provide simple code examples to make them easier to understand.

Another useful approach is to ask AI to explain the same concept in different ways. If one explanation is difficult to understand, a different example or comparison may make the idea clearer.

AI explanations are not always accurate, especially when dealing with complex programming concepts or unfamiliar technologies. Developers should verify important information before using it in their projects. Hallucination detection can help identify fabricated facts, incorrect technical explanations, and misleading information in AI-generated responses, making it easier to check the accuracy of what they learn.

This helps developers spend less time struggling with unfamiliar topics and more time building their technical knowledge.

Software development changes regularly. New frameworks, libraries, programming languages, and development methods continue to appear. Developers need to keep learning if they want to stay up to date.

AI can support this process by helping developers create learning plans based on their goals and current skills.

For example, a developer who wants to learn Python can ask AI to create a beginner-friendly learning plan. The plan can include basic syntax, variables, loops, functions, object-oriented programming, and small projects.

AI can also recommend practical exercises for each topic. Instead of only reading about a programming concept, developers can write code and test their understanding.

Here are some ways to use AI when learning new technologies:

However, developers should not depend entirely on AI-generated explanations. They should also read official documentation and test examples themselves. This helps them understand how technologies work in real development environments.

AI can help developers improve their coding skills by providing examples, explaining different solutions, and identifying areas that need improvement.

For example, a developer may write a function that works but contains unnecessary steps. They can ask AI to review the code and suggest ways to make it easier to read, maintain, or understand.

AI can also explain why one solution may be better than another. This allows developers to learn different approaches instead of always following the first solution they find.

Some practical ways to use AI for coding improvement include:

Developers can also ask AI to create small coding challenges based on their skill level. For example, someone learning Python can request exercises about lists, dictionaries, loops, and functions.

The important thing is to understand the code instead of copying it without review. Developers who examine the logic behind each solution can improve their programming knowledge over time.

Developers learn new information from many sources, including online courses, technical blogs, documentation, tutorials, and coding projects. Without a proper system, it can become difficult to find useful information when they need it again.

AI can help developers organize this knowledge and make learning resources easier to review.

For example, developers can use AI to summarize long technical explanations, create revision questions, and organize important programming concepts into smaller topics. They can also turn their learning notes into structured study guides that make it easier to revisit important information.

A well-organized knowledge system can be useful when learning a new framework or preparing for technical interviews. Instead of searching through old browser tabs or reading the same documentation repeatedly, developers can return to their saved explanations and notes.

Here are some useful ways to organize technical knowledge:

Technical documentation can contain detailed explanations that are difficult to remember. Developers can use AI to summarize important sections and turn them into short notes.

For example, when learning a new API, they can save information about its main functions, parameters, common errors, and practical examples.

Reading information does not always mean remembering it. Developers can ask AI to create questions from their notes so they can test their understanding.

For example, after learning about database indexing, they can create questions about how indexes work, when to use them, and how they affect query performance.

Developers should also save important information about their projects. This may include coding decisions, API details, database structures, and solutions to common problems.

Keeping these details organized makes it easier to return to a project after a break or help another developer understand the work.

Developers spend a large part of their working time on tasks that do not always require complex problem-solving. These may include writing basic code structures, creating test cases, preparing documentation, and handling repeated coding patterns.

AI can help reduce this manual effort by generating suggestions and automating parts of these tasks.

For example, when starting a new project, developers often need to create similar code structures, such as basic functions, configuration files, and reusable components. An AI coding assistant can generate an initial version that developers can review and adjust.

Automating these activities gives developers more time to focus on important parts of their projects, such as system design, complex features, and problem-solving.

However, generated code should always be checked before it is added to a project. Developers need to make sure it follows project requirements, coding standards, and security rules.

Finding and fixing bugs is an important part of software development. Even experienced developers can spend hours trying to understand why a program is not working as expected.

AI can help make debugging easier by explaining error messages, identifying possible causes, and suggesting solutions.

For example, when a developer encounters a Python error, they can share the relevant code and error message with an AI assistant. The assistant can explain what the error means and suggest possible ways to fix it.

AI can also help developers review code before submitting it. It may identify common issues such as:

Another useful approach is to ask AI to explain why a particular bug occurs instead of only requesting a corrected version of the code.

This helps developers understand the problem and avoid making the same mistake in future projects.

Still, AI suggestions are not always correct. Developers should test proposed fixes, review the surrounding code, and confirm that the solution does not introduce new problems.

Managing several development tasks at once can be difficult. Developers may need to work on new features, fix bugs, review code, attend meetings, and meet project deadlines.

AI can help organize these responsibilities by breaking large tasks into smaller and more manageable steps.

For example, if a developer needs to build a user authentication system, they can ask AI to divide the work into separate tasks. These may include creating registration forms, setting up database tables, implementing login logic, adding password protection, and testing the system.

This makes it easier to understand the work involved and decide what needs attention first.

AI can also help explain technical requirements before development begins. This may reduce confusion and help developers identify missing details early.

However, AI-generated plans should be treated as starting points. Developers still need to consider their actual deadlines, technical limitations, and project requirements before following them.

Although AI offers many benefits, depending on it for every programming task can affect a developer's ability to solve problems independently.

If developers always ask AI to write code, fix errors, and explain every concept, they may miss opportunities to develop their own technical skills.

A 2026 Anthropic study found that participants using AI scored 17 percentage points lower on a programming knowledge quiz than participants who worked without AI in the experiment. This highlights why understanding the work still matters when using coding assistants.

Developers can avoid excessive dependence on AI by following a few simple practices:

When facing a coding problem, spend some time understanding it and trying possible solutions. If you get stuck, use AI to explore the issue rather than asking it to complete everything.

Never add AI-generated code to a project without understanding what it does. Review the logic, check the functions, and test the output.

AI can sometimes provide outdated information, incorrect code, or explanations that do not fit a particular project. Check important details against official documentation and reliable technical resources.

Regular coding practice without assistance helps developers maintain their problem-solving skills. It also shows whether they truly understand a programming concept.

The best approach is to use AI as a helpful assistant while keeping independent thinking and technical judgment at the center of development work.

Using AI occasionally can be helpful, but developers can get more value from it by making it part of a regular learning and working routine.

A simple daily routine can help developers balance their project responsibilities with continuous learning.

For example, developers can follow this approach:

Start with a learning goal: Spend some time understanding a new programming concept, framework, or technology. Use AI to explain difficult topics and provide practical examples.

Plan the day's development tasks: Ask AI to help organize important tasks and break complex work into smaller steps.

Use AI during development: Get help with unfamiliar code, debugging, test cases, and repetitive tasks. Review all suggestions before using them.

Save useful information: Keep important explanations, coding examples, and solutions in an organized knowledge base for future reference.

Review what you learned: At the end of the day, revisit important concepts and test your understanding through small questions or coding exercises.

Developers do not need to spend hours following this routine. Even a short period of focused learning each day can help them build knowledge while managing their regular development work.

AI is becoming a useful part of modern software development. It can help developers understand difficult concepts, learn new technologies, improve code quality, debug problems, and complete repetitive tasks more efficiently.

However, better productivity does not simply mean writing more code in less time. Developers also need to understand what they are building, improve their problem-solving skills, and keep learning as technology changes.

The most effective approach is to use AI for support rather than letting it make every decision. By combining AI assistance with regular practice, independent thinking, and organized learning, developers can improve both their technical skills and everyday productivity.

#10499. Jensen Huang has argued execs need less supervision. Then a scandal made him step down as Nvidia CEO

The spectacular downfall of superstar Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—who resigned this morning after admitting to an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy and amid reports of another affair with one of his executives—casts a harsh light on a key tenet of Huang’s own management philosophy: that senior executives need little supervision.

Huang often used this belief to justify Nvidia’s unique management structure, in which 50 to 60 senior executives reported directly to him. He argued that senior leaders already have a proven ability to make decisions, manage people, and solve problems on their own.

“CEOs should have the most reports by definition, because the people that report to the CEO require the least amount of management,” he said during an appearance at Stanford Graduate School of Business in 2024. “It makes no sense to me that CEOs have so few people reporting to them.”

The approach, which Huang often reiterated in public appearances, reflects a broader Silicon Valley ideal: hire extraordinary people and give them free rein to do their best work. A classic example is Google’s 20%-time policy, which allowed employees to spend a portion of their time exploring their own ideas and innovations.  

Huang’s abrupt exit shows the drawbacks of this philosophy—at least when it comes to the behavior of top executives. While experienced leaders may not require micromanagement, allowing them to operate with very little oversight exposes organizations to major risks.

As Huang’s actions have illustrated, even the most capable executives can show extremely poor personal judgment. This may be especially true in corporate cultures like Nvidia’s, where the line between the personal and the professional is often blurred. 

Over the years, reports have described Nvidia as an intensely personal workplace in which Huang regularly interrogated junior employees about their work, sent emails late into the night, and exerted enormous influence over the company’s culture.

Senior leaders also have fewer people who are willing to rein in their behavior—something that was clearly the case at Nvidia. Last spring, proxy advisory firm Institutional Shareholder Services assigned its riskiest rating to Nvidia’s board structure. According to The Wall Street Journal, ISS cited the board’s multiple long-tenured directors, its lack of a chairman, the absence of a mechanism to refresh the board, and other factors.

Finally, the consequences of misconduct increase with seniority. In Huang’s case, the fallout could extend even beyond Nvidia, which manufactures chips crucial to the AI boom and has been central to American leadership in the area.

Management theorists have long struggled to balance meaningful oversight with executives’ autonomy, and some have concluded that no one-size-fits-all approach ensures proper board oversight. Boards must tailor oversight to individual CEOs and circumstances rather than mechanically apply standardized rules.

In Nvidia’s case, at least, the board of directors failed to properly assess the risks of Huang’s personal behavior or plan adequately for succession. And the lesson for others is clear: While senior executives don’t need micromanagement, they still need someone to answer to.

#10496. Everything you wanted to know about Nvidia but were too afraid to ask

If you’re not in the tech world, you might only have been vaguely aware of Nvidia—and CEO Jensen Huang’s leather jackets—until he admitted to having an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. On November 12, a day after revelations of a second affair, this one with an Nvidia executive, Huang resigned. Here’s why the company’s future could affect the entire AI industry.

What Nvidia does

Nvidia is at the center of the AI boom, as the world’s largest supplier of chips used in AI data centers. By some estimates, the company controls 80% of the market. As of November 3, it was the most valuable company in the world, with a market cap of around $5 trillion. By the morning of November 12, as Nvidia’s stock continued to plummet, that figure dropped to $4 trillion. (Huang’s own net worth had fallen $7.4 billion by that point.)

Huang and cofounders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem launched the company in 1993. They started making graphics processing units, better known as GPUs, for video games. In 2006, they rolled out a platform that enabled other uses for GPUs. In 2012, researchers used the company’s chips to train AlexNet, a breakthrough AI program that taught computers how to recognize images. By the time that ChatGPT launched, Nvidia’s tech was fundamental to AI development.

A large data center might have tens of thousands of Nvidia GPUs that run calculations to train AI models and generate responses when you type a question into ChatGPT or Claude. Training a new AI model could sometimes involve as many as 100,000 GPUs running at the same time for months. After the model is trained, the GPUs are used for “inference,” or applying the trained model to, say, rewrite your email or draw a cartoon of your cat. Inference also requires huge numbers of GPUs given that millions of people use AI at the same time. (In the U.S., around 60 million people use AI chatbots every day, according to a Pew survey this summer.)

Nvidia systems also include CPUs (central processing units) that coordinate tasks and run operating systems in data centers, along with networking equipment that lets GPUs communicate. Its software coordinates the GPUs.

Huang’s downfall

It’s not clear when Jensen Huang started his affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a woman who U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect of being a Chinese spy. The Chinese government has denied that she is a spy.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a senior executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that became an Nvidia customer. Megaspeed reportedly smuggled Nvidia’s chips into China, bypassing U.S. sanctions. The U.S. first restricted the export of Nvidia’s chips to China in 2022, citing the risk that China could use them for military development and to compete in AI. Alice Huang reportedly helped move $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to China.

The New York Times first reported on the relationship and the spy allegations on October 29, and Jensen Huang initially said that it was an ordinary business relationship, not an affair. On November 6, the Financial Times reported that it was a romantic relationship. Two days later, Jensen Huang sent an email to Nvidia employees admitting that it had been an affair.

On November 11, reports emerged that Huang also had an affair with one of his employees at Nvidia, reportedly Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare. On November 12, as pressure mounted from Nvidia’s board, Huang announced his resignation.

Why Jensen Huang can’t easily be replaced

It’s not simple for someone else to step into Huang’s shoes. He was directly involved in decisions that most executives would delegate, from managing in detail how Nvidia’s products were built to how salespeople talked to customers. A typical CEO might have five or 10 direct reports; Huang had as many as 60 direct reports. He reportedly sent hundreds of emails a day.

He had an unusual level of control—and no plan in place for succession. After Huang resigned, Nvidia CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO while the board searches for a replacement. It’s not clear what will happen next. But it’s possible that the company’s strategic decisions about products, manufacturing, and customers could slow down. Huang oversaw how Nvidia’s full system was integrated, not just its GPUs. The next leader may not have the same vision for the product. Relationships with customers might deteriorate. There might be internal struggles for control.

A circular business model—and potential fallout for AI companies

Nvidia sells its technology to companies like Microsoft, Amazon, and OpenAI. (OpenAI and others also use it indirectly by leasing space in third-party data centers.) But Nvidia is also investing heavily in the artificial intelligence ecosystem. It committed $30 billion to OpenAI’s financing round and guaranteed up to $105 billion for an Ohio data center that would serve OpenAI. It sells GPUs to AI infrastructure company CoreWeave, but has also invested in the company, including a $2 billion investment in January. Nvidia also agreed to purchase up to $6.3 billion of CoreWeave’s unused computing capacity over the next several years and has struck similar deals to buy cloud computing services from its customers. Meanwhile, it has partnered with Apollo, BlackRock, and other asset managers to mobilize financing for AI infrastructure.

Anthropic, which has plans to file for its IPO next week, is also tightly entangled with Nvidia. Nvidia committed to invest up to $10 billion in the company in 2025; Anthropic committed to use up to 1 gigawatt of Nvidia computing capacity. Nvidia was reportedly considering billions of dollars in credit guarantees for a new data center for Anthropic. It also had reported plans to invest up to $10 billion in Anthropic’s IPO.

All of this meant Nvidia was helping prop up demand for its own technology, making it harder to gauge how quickly AI would have grown on the strength of the underlying economics alone. Huang personally spearheaded these investments and partnerships, and it’s unclear whether his successor will be as willing to finance Nvidia’s customers. That uncertainty could slow some of the AI industry’s planned expansion.

#10494. Meta’s Horizon+ looks to become Meta VR+ and include 3D movies

Meta Horizon+ is rumored to be changing its name to Meta VR+ and may start including movies in addition to games with the subscription price.

Meta’s quest (ahem) to distance itself from the Horizon era is in full swing, and the latest rumor says it’s time for the company’s Game Pass-like subscription to change its brand name. VR leaker Nori posted a screenshot on X showing a handful of 3D movies coming to the Meta VR Plus service. Considering there is no such Meta VR Plus service currently, the obvious conclusion is that Meta Horizon+ is being renamed once again.

Meta Horizon+ currently includes over 100 games with its $7.99 per month subscription and is similar to Microsoft’s Xbox Game Pass service in many ways. Unironically, Meta Horizon+ also includes the basic Xbox Game Pass tier with over 50 Xbox games playable via the Game Pass cloud. Meta offers a 3-month trial with every new Meta Quest purchase.

The new Meta VR+ service is purported to include 3D movies as well, although we don’t yet know if this will be included in the regular $7.99 per month rate, or if Meta will be introducing additional content tiers, as services like Netflix, Disney+, Xbox Game Pass, and others do. Based on the screenshot, these will be big-name movies and are likely positioned to enhance the value of the upcoming $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, although all the same content will work on existing Meta Quest 3 units.

Meta has been slowly distancing itself from the “Horizon” name ever since the beginning of this year, when its VR division got a big reset. In a February blog post, Samantha Ryan, the VP of Content at Meta’s Reality Labs, spoke about the changes to the company’s strategy, including the loss of most in-house VR gaming studios. Since then, several prominent VR developers from Meta have gone on to create independent studios, including the super-popular Supernatural exercise app.

Meta then decoupled the unpopular Horizon Metaverse from its headsets, moving it to mobile-only, and has been removing the “Horizon” name from just about everything since then. Meta Horizon+ looks to be the latest big change, as the company moves toward “Meta VR” branding, which is clearer and separates its VR division from mobile and smart glasses efforts.

Intel and AMD NPU support is planned, but founder says neither will be used for language models.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A team led by Cyanogen co-founder Kirt McMaster has unveiled Kora, a new Linux desktop OS with integrated AI models and agents that can split workloads across CPU, GPU, and NPU resources, as well as other machines on the same local network. We reached out to the firm for more info.

Kora, the first product from Kora Systems Inc., previously Playtron, carries the tagline “The Operating System for Intelligence” and has its own Cortex “hybrid inference engine” technology, which is not open source and is optimized for local models. The OS, built “from the kernel to the shell,” runs local models by default and cloud models when needed, and is expected to arrive on PCs in 2027.

The desktop follows the AI-focused motif with “neural workspaces” and a “neural file system,” which refer to sandboxed workspaces and files indexed by semantic meaning. Kora has three operating modes: “Work," "Create," and "Play." That last base is covered by GameFrame, which descends from Playtron’s GameOS. Humain OS, which Kora is developing with Saudi AI company Humain, is the enterprise variant of this OS.

Currently, the only NPU named in the release material is the Hexagon NPU found in the Snapdragon X2 Elite, which Qualcomm pegs at 80 TOPS. On the X2 Elite, Cortex can schedule AI workloads across the CPU, GPU, and NPU, as well as other systems on the local network, which could be a novel capability if it works beyond the Qualcomm hardware.

McMaster told Tom’s Hardware that the Snapdragon X2 Elite NPU runs Google's Gemma 4 26B model at 25 tokens per second for decode. Intel and AMD NPU support is in the works, but according to the developer, neither NPU will be used for LLMs, as GPUs are “just better for LLM workloads on x64.”

Each NPU vendor has its own software stack, or runtime, and prefers that models are compiled in its own format: Qualcomm with QAIRT/QNN, Intel with OpenVINO, and AMD with Ryzen AI software. The press kit doesn't identify support for any Intel or AMD chip, NPU runtime, model format, quantization, or speed figures for those platforms.

Our earlier Windows testing showed the same kind of divide: Snapdragon reached its NPU through the QNN provider under ONNX Runtime, while Intel’s work ran through IPEX, its extension for PyTorch, on the GPU because it was faster than the NPU.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

When asked about cross-vendor support, McMaster reiterated that “only Hexagon on Snapdragon X2 Elite is supported today.” Intel NPU support is planned, with “conversations underway,” though McMaster later clarified that neither Intel’s nor AMD’s NPU will be used for LLMs. On AMD’s Ryzen AI chips, Kora will likely use the NPU for embedding and speech-recognition models through ONNX.As for what drives the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU, McMaster said Kora uses the “llama.cpp Hexagon backend” and “the upstream FastRPC driver.” That suggests the operating system reaches the NPU through the open-source llama.cpp project, not Qualcomm’s own QAIRT/QNN runtime, by way of the FastRPC driver in the mainline kernel.

Language models; KORA cites Gemma 4 26B at 25 tokens per second

Likely embedding and speech-recognition models; not language models

When asked about model formats, McMaster said, “we predominantly support GGUF,” llama.cpp’s model file format, and that Lemma, the inference engine inside Cortex, “can split model layers across processors as needed.” Lemma is built on llama.cpp, whisper.cpp, stable-diffusion.cpp, and ONNX. McMaster says that which runtime is used depends on the model's requirements, and more runtimes will be added down the line.

For today, llama.cpp has a Hexagon backend for Snapdragon and an OpenVINO backend for Intel CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, although the latter is still marked “In Progress,” and no AMD NPU backend, which would explain why AMD goes through ONNX. AMD NPUs can run LLMs on Linux through the separate Lemonade 10.0 stack with FastFlowLM, as reported by Phoronix in March, though that isn’t the route Kora has chosen.

Beyond NPU stacks, those hoping to run Kora will need to be mindful of their system's available memory. The Gemma 4 26B model Kora uses, which Google lists as Gemma 4 26B A4B, needs about 14.4GB of memory to load its weights at 4-bit (Q4_0) quantization, by Google’s estimate, before any context window, while third-party listings put the download for the Q4_K_M file Kora uses at about 16–17GB. The model only activates about 4 billion of its 26 billion parameters per token but still needs to be fully loaded into memory.

McMaster said that with the model, the X2 Elite reaches “25 TPS decode throughput and 550 TPS prefill throughput,” or tokens per second, running “entirely on the Hexagon NPU with 32K context.” A dense model, rather than a mixture-of-experts, would be far slower. Not given are the RAM configuration or the specific X2 Elite chip.

On memory, McMaster said that “we recommend 64GB because it gives you access to better models,” but that is not a firm requirement. The company projects that “about 70 percent of the model calls it manages will run locally in 2027.”

Kora says its enterprise-focused Humain OS is due first and will be “commercially available in 2027,” on OEM PCs using the Snapdragon X2 Elite. Kora will follow "later in 2027.”

McMaster says that “Kora will be posted on our site and downloadable for anyone to install.” Included will be a list of recommended configurations, “but it should be installable on most modern PCs.” Exact pricing and the overall business model will be shared closer to the date of availability.Edit: 11/11/2026 9:06am PT: Added further follow-up details provided by the maker.

#10492. The success KPIs nonprofits get right

Most organizations are built around a simple equation: Build a business, generate revenue, grow. I spent much of my career working within that equation, where success is often measured by familiar numbers: customers, dollars, CAGR.

Nonprofits start from a different premise. Their purpose is to advance a mission. And I have long argued that the clearest missions rarely have a true endpoint. An organization can work toward its goal for decades without ever being able to say, “We’re done.”

Measuring success can be more complex for nonprofits than for for-profit organizations. But in my work with the iF Design Foundation, a German nonprofit, I have found the opposite can also be true. When there is no ultimate finish line, you must be more intentional about why you do the work and how progress and success get measured.

A CLEAR PURPOSE MAKES DECISIONS SIMPLER

When growth is the primary objective, almost any decision can be justified so long as it pushes profits in an upward trajectory. Aaron Sorkin’s recent film depiction of Meta, The Social Reckoning, offers one take on what happens when that logic goes unchecked. But when the mission is the destination, a different question comes into focus: Does this decision support what we are ultimately here to achieve?

That question does not make difficult decisions easier, but it gives a clearer framework for making them.

I saw this firsthand when iF Design updated one of its annual iF DESIGN AWARD criteria three years back. We replaced the previous “Impact” criterion, which also included commercial considerations, with “Sustainability,” a framework tailored to the most relevant social and environmental factors in each of the award’s design categories. The criterion accounts for one-fifth of the total entry score, making iF the only international design award known to fully integrate these factors into its primary jurying criteria.

Changing an established system required rethinking the underlying jurying premise of “what makes great design?” and bringing sustainability experts from across disciplines and around the world into the process. There were logistical challenges and questions about implementation. Keeping the existing system would have been simpler. But our mission gave us a clear reason to move forward.

iF exists to advance design excellence and impact. If we believe design has a role to play in creating a better future for all, then sustainability invariably is part of how we evaluate it. The decision was not necessarily the easiest one. It was simply the decision most consistent with pursuing our purpose at this moment in time.

WITH NO ENDPOINT, DEFINE PROGRESS YOURSELF

In most for-profit companies, the scoreboard is largely handed to you. There may be debate over which numbers matter most, and differences based on ownership structures, industry, geography, etc., but the broad measures of success are usually understood.

A mission without a finish line comes with no such scoreboard. You have to decide what progress looks like.

I have found that more useful than disorienting. At iF, I think about growth less in terms of the organization’s size and more in terms of how many people engage with and are positively affected by its mission. Each year, tens of thousands of designers from around the world submit work to iF Design’s various award programs. But the number of entries matters less than what that participation makes possible: new ideas, objective feedback, and talent recognition, for starters.

This is a more strategic way to think about growth. The question is not simply whether the numbers are going up, but who is benefiting from our work.

WHAT FOR-PROFITS AND NONPROFITS CAN LEARN FROM EACH OTHER

Having spent years on both sides, I do not believe one model is inherently better. They serve different purposes and bring different offerings to the world. But after years as a senior marketer and operator focused on values-based brand building across the two, I would like to see the for-profit world start learning from the nonprofit world.

It all starts with purpose. A buzzword, yes, but fundamentally it is the question of “Why do we exist, and to what end?”

Purpose should not be an idea articulated after the business case has already been made. It should help determine whether the business case makes sense in the first place. For brand builders, that means treating mission and values as a starting point for decision-making, not simply as marketing messages. Done well, this approach can also strengthen brand loyalty and customer advocacy.

That is perhaps the biggest shift in perspective the nonprofit model has given me. Because in the for-profit world, nearly every problem depends on the answer to the question, “Will this grow the business?”

This is not to imply that revenue, profit, and growth are unimportant. Every organization needs to create enough value to sustain itself, and nonprofits are no exception. But when purpose is clear, money becomes a means rather than the primary destination.

When you understand what growth makes possible for the people you serve and the wider world, it becomes much easier to know whether you are moving in the right direction.

Lisa Gralnek is U.S. managing director and global head of sustainability at iF DESIGN, and host of the award-winning podcast FUTURE OF XYZ.

#10488. ‘You’ve Got Mail’ is getting a remake. There’s just one problem with that: Everything!

There are plenty of reasons to not remake a movie. Maybe it’s a stone-cold classic that seemingly can’t be improved upon. Sometimes it’s a foreign film that worked well enough already without photoshopping American faces into the lead roles. Other times, it’s an older movie with a recognizable title that nobody actually cares about anymore or one made so recently that remaking it serves no discernible purpose. These are all legitimate critiques, yet studios enamored with intellectual property frequently ignore them—with varying artistic and box office success.

You’ve Got Mail is a different situation altogether. 

While it’s perhaps impossible to replicate the star wattage, irresistible charm, and effortless chemistry of 1998 Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan, or the whip-smart comedic precision of filmmaker Nora Ephron (RIP), that isn’t even the main strike against a remake. Never mind that You’ve Got Mail reunited this trio five years after their funny, tearjerking smash, Sleepless in Seattle, giving it the rom-com equivalent of a Marvel movie’s magnitude. What makes You’ve Got Mail uniquely un-remake-able is that technology, social norms, and economics have changed so much in the last 28 years that everything about this movie now feels like a relic of the distant past.

Gen Z moviegoers—currently, the most active and coveted demographic—have likely never even heard the AOL notification that lent You’ve Got Mail its name. (It finally faded away for good last year when AOL discontinued its dial-up internet service, but the audio file had fallen out of cultural relevance sometime in the early-aughts.) If the words “You’ve got mail” now mean anything to young people, it’s likely in the context of “That old movie my parents like.”

An extremely 1998 film

Title aside, not much is known about the new Warner Bros. project. It will be directed by Jason Orley, the creative visionary behind the Pete Davidson-led Peacock series Bupkis, but plot details have yet to be announced. Possibly because those details threaten to turn the new film into something bearing scant resemblance to the original.

You’ve Got Mail, itself a remake of 1940’s The Shop Around the Corner (starring Jimmy Stewart and Margaret Sullavan), is centered around Kathleen Kelly (Ryan), an idealistic Upper West Side independent bookstore owner, and Joe Fox (Hanks), the cynical scion of a Barnes & Noble-like bookstore dynasty. The pair meet anonymously in an AOL chatroom, those early precursors to social media, and strike up a tastefully flirty friendship that drives them to consider leaving their current romantic partners (Greg Kinnear and Parker Posey, respectively). The dynamics of their quasi-courtship change, however, when Fox realizes his unnamed potential paramour is actually the woman his new store on the Upper West Side is about to put out of business. It’s a Montagues-and-Capulets-caliber obstacle that forestalls the inevitable happy ending.

The plot of this warm blanket of a movie hinges on two intertwined ideas: that strangers can connect over the internet and not turn out to be creeps, and that enormous chain bookstores are the mortal enemy of independents. Both ideas now seem quaintly, adorably naive.

Dating? On the internet??

In 1998, the internet was a mysterious novelty. Only 41% of adults had even logged on at all. While early adopters swore it would eventually change everything, most Americans were still wrapping their heads around the concept of email. Now, of course, the internet is the infrastructure modern society is built upon, and the filter through which many people experience the world. About 97% of adults younger than 50 are now connected to it at all times through smartphones, a technology that was nearly a decade away when You’ve Got Mail was made.

In retrospect, it’s a miracle that a person of Nora Ephron’s age—she was 56 at the time—perfectly depicted the moment when meeting strangers on the internet first broached mainstream acceptability. Prior to then, meeting people online was considered sordid, shameful business. Ephron both grounded her film in that perception and circumvented it by having her two leads fall ass-backward into internet romance.

There was something interesting and even sort of sweet about the idea of potential soulmates accidentally finding each other within the randomness of a nonsexual Web 1.0 chatroom. It now sounds like the kind of meet-cute one of those elderly couples in the Ephron-penned When Harry Met Sally might share if that film came out today.

What could possibly be an organic way for two attached people in 2026, though, to accidentally strike up a relationship online that retains the innocent curiosity of the 1998 internet? 

There’s nothing interesting anymore about meeting someone online. A chance encounter with a stranger on the r/Pringles subreddit could potentially lead to a hookup, which is something everyone has known or at least intuited for a very long time. Internet dating is now well past mainstream status. It’s something so pervasive as to no longer require any hand-wringing or soul-searching—you either do it or don’t do it, and nobody cares much either way. According to a 2019 study from Stanford University, over 39% of heterosexual couples now meet online, making the internet the most popular destination for sparking a new relationship.

But even if the filmmakers found a plausible scenario in which the two leads chastely meet online, they won’t face the dilemma that occupies the first half of the original movie—whether to physically meet someone who digitally swept you off your feet. After multiple decades of normalized internet dating, that question no longer carries any tension. Without it, the remake will just be about whether two people in unfulfilling relationships should turn their emotional infidelity into something more—essentially the plot of any generic romantic comedy.

Borders: Now there’s a name I haven’t heard in a long time

Although You’ve Got Mail correctly portrays the two leads’ ongoing anonymity as a red flag, the mutual identity firewall makes sense given the pair’s hesitation to go any further. But the idea that both parties in a more modern online flirtation would emotionally invest several months in someone who insists on keeping their identity a secret is ludicrous.

Even harder to pull off in a modern update than keeping their identities secret is who the two main characters actually are offline.

In 1998, an indie bookseller going up against a big-box bookstore would have been a genuine David-and-Goliath conflict. Barnes & Noble and Borders represented an existential threat to any local shop who struggled to keep up with the bottomless inventory, discounted pricing, and piping hot coffee those chains had in spades. Little did either side know they’d soon be united together in a battle for brick-and-mortar bookstore survival against Amazon, which launched just three years before You’ve Got Mail.

Now, all bookstores are fighting for their lives, with Barnes & Noble cribbing notes from indie bookshops to stay relevant in the BookTok era. (Borders did not survive Amazon’s ascendance, having reached its final chapter back in 2011.)

Affinity for independent booksellers was no match for the convenience and savings of a Barnes & Noble back in 1998, which is why Kelly eventually loses her shop in the film. That’s no longer necessarily the case. Anyone setting foot in a bookshop now has generally made an intentional choice to not buy a book from Amazon for cheap, and to instead experience human curation and customer service while supporting a local business. Meanwhile, Barnes & Noble is now more likely to buy a struggling independent bookshop than put one out of business.

The only way the major conflict in You’ve Got Mail would work in a modern update is if the plot moved out of the book world entirely, which is what will likely happen. But current options for a David-and-Goliath-esque business conflict that poignantly capture a changing world, mid-transformation, aren’t exactly inspiring. Maybe it will involve a celebrity podcaster at a major network launching a new show with the exact same idea as a well-established indie podcast—a concept I’m already mad about just having thought of. Maybe it will be the creator of a hot new AI chatbot financially ruining the founder of a once-great search engine. It might even be something even dumber. Unfortunately, the resulting movie could accidentally provide some incisive metacommentary about the moment “enshittification” came for Hollywood. 

Whatever happens, any remake of You’ve Got Mail that’s even vaguely faithful to the source material will have a title that no longer has any meaning, a premise that no longer matters, and a conflict that no longer exists. 

The only way to fix these problems would be to change so much about the original that what’s mainly being remade is the definition of what can reasonably be considered a remake. At that point, why not just start from scratch? The resounding box office lesson of 2026 is that audiences are tired of being treated like seals who reliably clap at the dangled fish of familiar IP. Original hits like Obsession, You Can See Everything, and The Drama inspired as much conversation this year as they did box office returns. 

Unrecognizable remakes of beloved classics, on the other hand, seem more like the modern descendants of another relic of the late 1990s: the straight-to-video sequel.

#10485. How Motion Design Improves SaaS Onboarding and Feature Adoption

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most SaaS products don't lose users because the software is bad. They lose users in the first few minutes, before anyone has seen what the product can actually do. Someone signs up, lands on an empty dashboard, feels a flicker of confusion, and quietly leaves. The industry has a name for the gap between signing up and getting value: activation. Closing it is one of the hardest problems in product design.

Motion design is one of the most underused tools for closing that gap. Used well, animation isn't decoration sprinkled on at the end. It's a layer of communication that tells users where to look, confirms that their actions worked, and makes a complex interface feel learnable instead of overwhelming. This article looks at why motion influences behaviour during onboarding, the specific patterns that move the needle on activation and feature adoption, and how to build them responsibly as a developer — with an eye on performance and accessibility throughout.

Motion works in onboarding because it speaks to how human perception actually operates, not because it looks modern. A few principles do most of the heavy lifting.

It directs attention. The eye is drawn to movement before it reads a single word. A gently pulsing button or an element that slides into view tells a new user where to go next without a paragraph of instructions. On a crowded first-run screen, that guidance is the difference between a confident first action and a confused exit.

It preserves context. When a panel expands, a card flips, or a new view slides in from the right, a short transition shows users where things came from and where they went. This spatial continuity keeps people oriented. Interfaces that snap instantly between states force the user to re-scan the screen each time and silently rebuild their mental model.

It confirms actions. Every click, toggle, and form submission is a small question: did that work? A quick visual response — a checkmark drawing itself, a row settling into place — answers it immediately. Without that feedback, users repeat actions, doubt the system, or assume something broke.

It shapes perceived performance. A thoughtful loading animation or skeleton screen makes a wait feel shorter and the product feel responsive, even when the underlying request takes exactly as long. Perception of speed is part of the experience, and motion is how you manage it.

These are the patterns that reliably help new users reach their first win.

Onboarding doesn't end after the first session. Most SaaS products keep shipping features, and each one faces its own adoption problem: users settle into a few familiar workflows and never discover the rest. Motion is how you reintroduce the product to people who already think they know it.

Contextual nudges that appear in motion — a tooltip that eases in near a newly relevant button, a gentle highlight on a feature the moment a user hits the limit it solves — are far more effective than a generic email. They arrive at the point of need and use movement to pull attention without hijacking the screen.

"What's new" reveals can announce an update with a small, well-timed animation rather than a modal that gets dismissed on reflex. A badge that animates in, or a panel that slides open on the first visit to a page, respects the user's flow while still being noticed.

Animated demonstrations carry the most weight for genuinely complex features. Showing a feature in motion — rather than describing it in text — lets users grasp a multi-step workflow in seconds. For intricate capabilities, this is where a short, purpose-made explainer earns its place, a point we return to in the next section.

The right tool depends on how complex the animation is and where it lives. Roughly in order of weight:

CSS transitions and keyframe animations should be your default. They cover the large majority of onboarding motion — hovers, state changes, highlights, progress bars — and the browser can run them efficiently. Reach for JavaScript only when CSS genuinely can't express what you need.

The Web Animations API gives you CSS-level performance with programmatic control, which matters when animations depend on data or user input, or need to be sequenced and interrupted. SitePoint's guide to the Web Animations API is a solid introduction, and the broader web animation archive covers libraries like GSAP for orchestrating complex timelines.

Lottie is the bridge between designer-made animation and the web. Designers export vector animations as JSON, and a lightweight player renders them natively at small file sizes — ideal for polished illustrative moments like success states and animated empty states, without hand-coding every frame.

Pre-rendered video is the right call when a feature is genuinely involved and a looping CSS animation or a tooltip simply can't carry the explanation. A short, well-produced walkthrough can compress a multi-step workflow into something a user absorbs in under a minute, which is why many teams lean on a dedicated SaaS explainer video for their most complex features and onboarding moments. The trade-off is weight and production effort, so reserve video for the handful of places where it genuinely outperforms in-interface motion, lazy-load it, and never autoplay it with sound.

Motion that stutters does more damage than no motion at all, and motion that ignores accessibility can actively harm users. Two disciplines keep animation on the right side of that line.

For performance, animate the properties the browser can handle cheaply: transform and opacity. These can run on the compositor thread without triggering layout or paint, which is what lets animation hold a smooth 60fps. Animating properties like width, height, top, or left forces the browser to recalculate layout on every frame and is the usual cause of janky motion. Keep animations short — most interface transitions should land between 150 and 300 milliseconds — because motion that overstays its welcome makes a product feel slow.

For accessibility, honour the prefers-reduced-motion media query. Some users experience dizziness, nausea, or disorientation from movement, and the operating system lets them ask for less of it. Respecting that setting is straightforward:

Beyond that, never let an animation block interaction. If a user has to wait for a flourish to finish before they can click, the motion is working against them. Animation should support the task and then get out of the way.

Motion design is a product decision, so treat it like one and measure it. The metrics that matter map directly to the problems motion is meant to solve.

Treat animations as hypotheses and A/B test them. Ship the animated onboarding step to half of your new users and measure activation against the control. Motion should earn its place with data, not assumptions — and occasionally the data will tell you an animation is slowing people down, which is just as useful to know.

The best onboarding motion is the kind users never consciously notice. It simply makes the product feel clear, responsive, and easy to learn — guiding attention, confirming actions, and turning a complex interface into something approachable. That's the real payoff: not animation for its own sake, but fewer confused users, faster time to value, and features that actually get discovered.

Start small. Pick the single point in your onboarding where users most often stall, add one purposeful animation that removes the confusion, and measure what happens. Motion, used deliberately, is one of the most direct levers you have on activation and adoption — and like any good tool, it works best when it draws no attention to itself.

Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), the chairperson of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has said that he will issue a subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he does not respond to the committee’s request to meet with them on November 18 by Wednesday, November 11, according to ABC News. The House invited him to a “joint, closed-door briefing” with the heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence, and that they will focus on his company’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage.”

Congress first called the embattled CEO on November 7, a few days after rumors started circulating about Huang’s “closeness” to a particular Chinese executive suspected of passing information to Chinese intelligence. The following day, Nvidia released a statement from Jensen admitting to an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, apologizing for his unfaithfulness, while the company’s board of directors confirmed it will launch an independent investigation regarding the allegations that the CEO has been specifically targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS). Aside from having to face Congress, Jensen Huang is also reportedly being looked into by the FBI.

It remains unclear whether Jensen Huang was targeted by intelligence agencies, but he came into prominence with the AI boom that was arguably fueled by Nvidia’s AI chips. This led to the AI race as we know it today, with the U.S. taking steps to delay China’s advancement for fears that it will use the technology for military purposes. We also don’t know if Huang Le or Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy or an “innocent” bystander caught in a web of accusations. And, even if she did work with the MSS, the question remains as to whether she specifically targeted the Nvidia CEO or whether Chinese intelligence discovered their indiscretion and used that as a convenient tool for blackmail to extract information from her.

However, former CIA agent Darrel Blocker told ABC News that the authorities should just focus on Jensen. “I think that the biggest concern is that the focus or overfocus on just Jensen Huang and Nvidia risks losing sight of the fact that other people have been targeted by the Chinese. Are they talking to the engineers? Are they talking to other people who might have even more access than even the CEO has? So, this focus should not be singular; it should include everyone in the company, and quite frankly, every tech company out there should be looking at all the contacts that their officers and employees have.”

“It’s definitely not a one-time thing. When you run a trillion-dollar company, you know that you have a bullseye on your back; whether it’s from competition or rather from nation-states, so this is absolutely not a one-off. Jensen Huang is not the only person at Nvidia that has access to the crown jewels, so I would be looking at the other people in terms of the access that they enjoy and their proximity to Chinese nationals.”

#10481. How the effects of Jensen Huang’s ouster are spiraling out through the economy

Nvidia and Jensen Huang aren’t the only ones in the crosshairs. 

The longtime tech executive has had a bad week. It all began when news surfaced that Huang had been having an extramarital affair with an alleged spy for the Chinese government. In response, the corporate board of Nvidia—the company Huang cofounded more than 30 years ago—began an investigation. The FBI launched a probe, too. Then news broke Wednesday that Huang had engaged in at least one other affair, this time with a company executive who reported directly to him.

By Thursday morning, Huang had resigned, and the chip company had appointed an interim CEO. But the hits kept coming. Thursday afternoon Reuters reported that Huang had engaged in an affair with a second employee.

Obviously, this is bad news for Nvidia. Stocks are down, and Democrats, now preparing to take back Congress, appear to be ramping up plans to investigate the company and any possible risks to U.S. national security. But this is also bad for a range of other entities that have a stake in Nvidia’s success.

Here are a few that stand to feel some of the blowback. 

The White House

The White House, fresh off of devastating losses in the midterm elections, stands to face questions about why it held off on taking action after it learned about Huang’s affair with an alleged spy. The Trump administration already had a poor reputation for security and intelligence practices, but seemingly sleeping on this knowledge is all but certain to raise the prospect of further probes. 

Trump officials, notably, have cleared deals allowing Nvidia to sell advanced computer chips to China, and even leveraged U.S. influence over the company’s chips in geopolitical negotiations. 

Current and prospective NVIDIA customers

The U.S. AI supply chain runs on Nvidia. OpenAI, Anthropic, and a slew of other large language model developers rely on the company’s hardware. Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are also major customers. This is, in large part, because GPUs—or graphics processing units—are particularly adept at the kinds of computations needed to develop large reasoning models. 

Now, with so much scrutiny on Nvidia, there’s a risk those companies—and any deals in progress—might face headwinds as the still-scrambling board figures out what to do next. The Semiconductor Industry Association, a major trade group that advocates for chip companies, declined to comment. Hugging Face, an AI developer that agreed to an acquisition by Nvidia earlier this year, did not respond to a request for comment. 

Remarkably, Huang doesn’t seem to have had a succession plan. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was appointed interim CEO on Thursday morning. 

The scandal and disarray isn’t just bad for American companies that need Nvidia’s chips. Given the extent to which Huang advocated for loosening chip sale limits to China, any customers with suspected links to the Chinese government may also see far more scrutiny on Nvidia deals than before. 

U.S. federal agencies

The U.S. government is a major supporter of Nvidia, using the company’s tech extensively in its own systems, including classified networks. The revelations this week are not only embarrassing for the government, but raise concerns about the extent to which government officials were aware of Huang’s affair with a suspected spy for China, and how they might have influenced the company’s dealings with federal agencies.

One former federal chief information officer told Fast Company that the scandal raises suspicions that the U.S. security clearance system, which is supposed to engage in continuous monitoring, isn’t as up to snuff as it should be. 

Everyone else 

We really are that dependent on Nvidia. If we learned anything from the chip shortage we experienced during the pandemic, the semiconductor market is heavily concentrated, and disruptions with just one company can quickly ripple through the economy. In 2020, it was companies like TSMC, a Taiwan-based contract manufacturer that supplies chips for a host of devices. And the stock market—including pension funds and 401(k) plans—are deeply exposed to Nvidia stock.

“It is striking that Nvidia, a $4 trillion company central to both the AI economy and U.S. equity markets, appears to have no publicly identified successor to Jensen Huang,” Ann Lewis, a technology executive and former U.S. government tech official, told Fast Company Wednesday. “In cybersecurity, we call this a single point of failure. A company of this scale should not depend so completely on one person’s relationships and judgment.”

#10480. Trump’s suggestion for the next Nvidia CEO is another tech titan he’s already close with

With Jensen Huang officially out as president and CEO of Nvidia, rumors are swirling over who will take his place at the helm of one of the world’s biggest tech companies. Could it be interim CEO Colette Kress, who’s spent more than a decade as Nvidia’s executive vice president and CFO? Or maybe company cofounder Chris Malachowsky, now a senior vice president of engineering and operations?

President Donald Trump has his own idea. His left-field pick: former Apple CEO Tim Cook. In a post on Truth Social, Trump announced his preference for Huang’s successor.

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”

Beyond Trump’s dubious claim that Huang did “a fantastic job” as CEO—having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy might disqualify him from that distinction—Cook is far from an obvious pick to step into the role.

Cook only recently transitioned out of his CEO role at Apple, becoming the company’s executive chairman in September. In a meeting announcing the decision, Cook spelled out the considerations that allowed for the shift: The “business had to be doing great,” the “product road map [had] to be incredible,” and his replacement, former senior vice president of hardware engineering John Ternus, had to be “ready for the role.” With all those conditions met, “now was the time,” Cook said.

Why, then, would Trump want Cook to take on another CEO mantle? Notably, the two have gotten close during Trump’s second term as president.

Trump and Cook, sitting in a tree

Trump and Cook weren’t always buddies. During Trump’s first term, he infamously referred to Cook as “Tim Apple,” seemingly forgetting his name.

But since Trump took back the office in 2025, Cook has frequently been spotted at the president’s side, from attending a White House dinner for tech CEOs last September to watching an early screening of first lady Melania Trump’s documentary in early 2026.

For his part, Cook insists he’s not politically aligned with Trump, instead abstaining from politics entirely.

“What I do is I interact on policy, not politics. I’m not a political person on either side. I’m not political,” Cook said in an interview with Good Morning America earlier this year. “I’m kind of straight down the middle. And I focus on policy, so I’m very pleased that the president and the administration is accessible to talk about policy.”

That purported focus on policy aligns with Cook’s intentions for his role as Apple’s executive chairman, which include overseeing the company’s global relations. “This is an area where we’ve built relationships over multiple years . . . and I think I can help with that,” Cook said when announcing his step-down.

A support page on Motorola’s website lists the name of the device as “Razr Flex,” a name we’ve previously heard in connection with this wide form factor, while the page also directly says that the device is a 2027 release. There’s no firm release date, but it’s almost certainly not arriving before the end of the year, despite initial leaks around Motorola’s wide foldable hinting at a 2026 release.

The Motorola “Razr Flex” is expected to have a very compact form factor and, based on Motorola’s initial plans, will likely have 3D glass and at least wants to have a creaseless display, seemingly with just two cameras on the back similar to Apple and Samsung’s wide foldables. The outer display might be a mere 4.97-inch panel, much smaller than others.
