#10474. Cognichip reveals how its new AI-assisted program can slash chip design times from months to days — automating labor-intensive tasks cuts design time down, Chief Product Officer explains

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

We speak to Cognichip's Chief Product Officer, Stelios Diamantidis, about its new AI products

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Amid the AI gold rush, one particularly fruitful vein of research is the emergence of AI-assisted workflows in electronic design automation (EDA) tools like Cadence Maestro. One such company developing such foundational models is Cognichip, which in September launched Artificial Chip Intelligence (ACI), proprietary AI models developed specifically for semiconductor engineering. ACI deploys the 'industry’s largest training dataset' across semiconductor physics and chip design principles.

ACI Enterprise is Cognichip's deployable platform, which combines these specialized models with agentic workflows, project memory, and computing infrastructure for AI inference. The company describes ACI's approach as a self-learning flywheel, a continuously evolving design environment that brings together specifications, register-transfer level (RTL), and verification results to build a design that meets power, performance, and area (PPA) targets to Pareto limits. We sat down with Cognichip to learn more.

"We have surpassed, I think, over ten million training samples in our datasets that are either things that we designed ourselves directly or things that have been generated through our synthetic technology," says Stelios Diamantidis, Chief Product Officer at Cognichip, in an interview with Tom's Hardware Premium. "We have invented new ways of creating synthetic training samples for semiconductor design. And very importantly, now that we have all these data samples, characterized data samples, we also had to invent new models so that we can capture the data, and we also had to invent new pipelines for training so that we can map the training data to the models themselves."

Cognichip says ACI can analyze specifications, explore microarchitectural options, generate RTL, verify designs, identify and fix functional problems, and optimize designs to meet PPA targets. The system can also integrate existing IP modules and even produce FPGA implementations. In principle, ACI enables engineers to focus on product requirements and architectural decisions while ACI handles much of the logic implementation and verification work.

"Build the spec, build the RTL, estimate PPA, perform optimizations, run verification, everything," Diamantidis told us while explaining how ACI can develop and evaluate multiple architectural alternatives before engineers select the preferred design. "We do not try to turn the designer into a verification engine; our system is self-verified, so we want the designer to design, and we want our system not only to do the tasks but also verify them."

Because ACI operates as a self-learning flywheel, Cognichip claims engineers can revisit earlier architectural decisions and modify their designs without restarting the entire development process from scratch.

"Architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, all abstractions in the cognitive system are aligned, so the change in microarchitecture is essentially automatically reflected in RTL, and vice versa," Diamantidis explained. "Changes in RTL are automatically reflected in microarchitecture."

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Cognichip says it has participated in more than 40 customer engagements, including projects at Renesas and SiTime. According to the company, these engagements span a wide range of chip designs, from microcontrollers and encryption engines to networking processors, RISC-V CPUs, and AI accelerators.

To illustrate ACI's capabilities, Cognichip points to an evaluation conducted with an unnamed leading fabless semiconductor company. The customer provided an existing 55-page microarchitecture specification, which ACI used to explore architecture options, develop RTL from scratch, and integrate middleware and other components. The system also generated SystemVerilog testbenches, ran simulations, identified and corrected errors, and achieved functional verification closure with over 90% UVM coverage, the company claims. According to Cognichip, the entire process took just 10 days and required only one engineer. By contrast, doing the same job using conventional methods would require a full front-end design team and approximately 20 weeks, Cognichip says.However, there are several important caveats. First up, the customer had already provided a detailed 55-page microarchitecture specification, so the platform did not begin with a blank sheet. Secondly, Cognichip has not disclosed the complexity of the design, which makes it difficult to assess how much work has been done (or rather, processed). Finally, the reported acceleration applies to front-end engineering rather than the entire chip development process, which also includes physical implementation, tape-out, manufacturing, and silicon validation.

There is a substantial difference between developing functionally, conducting verified RTL, and prepping a chip design for manufacturing. Although Cognichip's ACI can develop microarchitectures, generate RTL, and optimize designs for PPA, the platform does not perform physical implementation. Tasks such as floorplanning, placement and routing, clock-tree synthesis, physical verification, and signoff still require conventional electronic design automation (EDA) tools from companies like Cadence, Synopsys, and Siemens EDA.

"Today we do not do physical implementation," Diamantidis said. "So, place and route […] is done outside of our system."

This distinction matters because an architecture that meets its estimated PPA targets may fail to achieve them after physical implementation. For example, a design expected to operate at 1 GHz while consuming 15 W could achieve only 800 MHz at 20 W once engineers account for interconnect delays, clock distribution, buffering requirements, congestion, and other physical effects. Such discrepancies can require changes to RTL or even fundamental architectural elements, followed by another round of verification and physical implementation. In some cases, these iterations can consume weeks or months of engineering time.

"That cycle is very expensive in terms of time," Diamantidis said. "Because you are crossing design boundaries, and you are running very long runtimes and all that."

Cognichip claims that ACI can reduce these costly iterations by predicting the physical consequences of architectural decisions before implementation begins. According to Diamantidis, the company has trained its models on internally developed and characterized semiconductor designs, which enables ACI to estimate PPA characteristics and identify potential architectural trade-offs during front-end development.

"We have trained models with full physical stack visibility understanding so that the models can predict the PPA during the front-end design phase." "We can identify those trade-offs before going to physical implementation."

For example, ACI could recommend replacing two independent FIFOs with a single time-multiplexed FIFO to reduce power consumption at the expense of performance. Diamantidis used this hypothetical scenario to illustrate how the platform can evaluate architectural alternatives before engineers commit to a particular implementation.

"If you want to save power here at the cost of 10% of frequency, take these two FIFOs that you have for two different tasks, merge them, make one FIFO, and then time multiplex the two functions over one FIFO," Diamantidis explained.

Cognichip claims that ACI can estimate not only the immediate PPA consequences of such changes but also their potential impact on physical implementation.

"These trade-offs become visible now because we can tell the designer essentially in real time what some of these impacts are going to be to downstream parasitics and downstream congestion and all those kinds of effects."

The general idea behind ACI is to resolve potential architectural problems before RTL reaches physical design engineers rather than wait for implementation results and revise the architecture afterward.

"Our expectation is that there will be no loopbacks to the designer in terms of 'let us do this again because we did not meet this goal or because we ran into congestion issues,'" said Diamantidis.

However, the accuracy of these predictions is critical. Cognichip claims its models can predict certain PPA characteristics with errors of approximately 10% relative to results obtained from conventional EDA tools at the pre-route stage of physical implementation.

Cognichip evaluated its technology using 1,200 open-source designs and compared its predictions with those produced by general-purpose AI models, including Anthropic's Claude Opus and Google's Gemini. According to him, general-purpose models produced errors of approximately 50% – 100%, depending on the metric, whereas Cognichip's models reduced prediction errors to around 10%.

"[General purpose models] do not do well when it comes to predicting delays," Diamantidis said. "So, we take that down to within 10%. Again, 10% because think about it, we are running it at RTL. We do not have much physical information at all, right?"

There is an important distinction, though. Cognichip's reported accuracy refers to pre-route physical implementation results, not final post-route characteristics. Actual routing introduces interconnect and power delivery parasitics as well as other physical effects that can alter timing and power consumption. Consequently, the reported 10% prediction error does not necessarily mean that ACI-generated designs will achieve their estimated PPA targets after physical implementation and signoff.

Another question concerns the range of architectures and manufacturing technologies for which ACI can deliver such accuracy. Although Cognichip says its models incorporate semiconductor physics and account for process-dependent characteristics, it has not disclosed which foundry nodes it supports or how prediction accuracy varies across them.

Diamantidis explained that some architectural decisions are largely independent of manufacturing technology, whereas others become increasingly dependent on the target process node as development progresses.

"[Think about chip development as a tree], at the top of the tree, there are decisions that are not really foundry-specific; they are closer to microarchitecture," he explained. "Then, of course, as you start working your way down the tree, at some point you branch off because the decision may be targeted towards the TSMC node A versus TSMC node B, which will result in different prediction things. But there is a big trunk of decisions that are not really related to the node and are more related to the architecture and the way that the architecture is implemented. What we try to do is we try to think of this whole tree and provide a lot of feedback to designers, especially in a node-agnostic mode, and then, of course, at some point we have to become more node-aware."

This distinction is exceedingly important for complex CPUs, GPUs, and AI accelerators, where physical constraints tend to have substantial impact on architectural decisions. Meanwhile, Cognichip does not claim that ACI must develop such processors as monolithic designs. Instead, the company says its technology can work with individual IP blocks and subsystems, which engineers can subsequently integrate into larger chips. Of course, integration of these individually optimized IP blocks into larger chips is a challenge.

Although Cognichip says ACI can handle subsystems containing millions of logic gates (i.e., circuits that implement Boolean functions), combining multiple such designs into a complex SoC introduces additional constraints related to interconnect delays, clock distribution, shared memory bandwidth, power delivery, and floorplanning. Consequently, an architecture that achieves Pareto-optimal PPA characteristics as a standalone subsystem may no longer be optimal once integrated into a larger chip. According to Cognichip, ACI can account for these system-level interactions by aligning and optimizing individual blocks against global SoC and subsystem constraints.

“Yes, ACI can align and optimize individual blocks to global SoC and subsystem constraints. It can be applied to both flat and hierarchical optimization problems,” Diamanditis said.

Cognichip is not proposing a fundamentally new SoC development methodology, but rather automating substantial portions of conventional front-end workflows. Its ACI platform supports both flat and hierarchical optimization and can drive the partitioning and propagation of design constraints from the top level to individual blocks. According to Cognichip, ACI can decompose system-level constraints into requirements for individual components and then re-aggregate them as the blocks are integrated.

“ACI does not require a flat design methodology; it can drive hierarchical design from the top or subsystem-top down, ensuring that constraints are decomposed going into components but then re-aggregated when blocks are integrated,” Diamanditis explained.

According to Cognichip, ACI can handle individual IP blocks and subsystems containing millions of logic gates, which can subsequently be combined hierarchically into larger SoCs. The company emphasizes that the complexity of individual partitions, rather than their size, determines how effectively ACI can handle them. However, it remains to be seen how effectively ACI can coordinate architectural decisions and optimize PPA across an entire complex SoC in practice. After all, a Pareto-optimal CPU core, memory controller, and interconnect do not necessarily form a Pareto-optimal SoC, as their interactions introduce additional timing, bandwidth, power, and physical constraints.

Then again, developers of complex SoCs already address these challenges with hierarchical design methodologies, system-level optimization, and integration, so ACI’s focus on individual subsystems does not necessarily represent a significant limitation.

One of the questions that normally occurs when we talk about a tool that is only aimed at the front end of chip development is how it can handle feedback loops from physical implementation (more on this later). Such feedback loops occur when placement and routing reveal problems with timing, power consumption, die area, or routing congestion that cannot be resolved through physical design optimizations alone. In more serious cases, engineers must revise RTL, pipelines, memory hierarchies, or other architectural elements, which requires another round of functional verification, synthesis, and physical implementation. These iterations can take plenty of time and involve multiple engineering teams, which makes them particularly expensive.

Cognichip says ACI can use physical implementation results to revise RTL and microarchitecture if necessary, although this is not the company's primary focus. Instead, it aims to prevent costly iterations between front-end and back-end design teams by predicting potential problems before physical implementation begins.

"We are still focused very much on what we can do in the front end to prevent these situations rather than fix them."

If physical implementation reveals problems that require changes to RTL or microarchitecture, engineers can return to ACI with the relevant feedback (Cognichip does not specify with which file format that feedback must be submitted) and use the platform to revise their designs. Yet, ACI cannot resolve issues that require changes to the physical implementation itself, such as clock-tree synthesis or placement and routing.

"They can come back to our environments to provide additional guidance, additional prompting, additional information," Diamantidis said. "Then based on that information, we can of course perform an adaptation of the design […] if the issue can be addressed in the design itself, then of course we can do that."

Since feedback loops are expensive, yet necessary parts of semiconductor chip development flow, I had to ask that question explicitly, and the answer was that there would be no need for feedback loops with ACI. As the question and response require a lot of minutiae, we've added them in full below.

Anton Shilov: Can ACI ingest physical implementation reports from Cadence, Synopsys, or Siemens EDA tools, identify architectural bottlenecks, revise the microarchitecture, and RTL, and repeat the process until the design meets its PPA targets?

Stelios Diamantidis: Actually, this is where we depart from conventional approaches. We do not need to wait until physical implementation to identify these issues. We have trained models with full physical-stack visibility, which enables them to predict PPA during the front-end design phase.

For example, suppose you have one design that operates at a certain frequency and consumes a certain amount of power, and another that runs perhaps 20% slower but consumes significantly less power. We can identify these trade-offs before physical implementation.

Ultimately, the changes you want to make involve RTL and design constraints. Traditionally, engineers develop the RTL and constraints and hand them over to the physical implementation team. That team implements the design and reports the results. If the design fails to meet its targets, the front-end team must make changes, and the process starts again.

These iterations are very expensive in terms of time because they cross design boundaries and involve tools with long runtimes.

By training our models on the full physical stack, we can now provide immediate feedback to front-end designers. For example, we might tell an engineer: 'If you want to reduce power consumption at the cost of 10% of your frequency, take two FIFOs that serve different functions, combine them into one, and time-multiplex the two functions over that FIFO.'

That is just one example of a microarchitectural decision. We can make these trade-offs visible to designers in essentially real time because our models can predict their impact on downstream parasitics, routing congestion, and other physical characteristics.

As a result, engineers can make these decisions in a closed loop during front-end development. Once they have resolved the microarchitectural trade-offs and produced well-structured RTL, they can hand the design over to the physical implementation team. Of course, the design still has to go through physical implementation tools.

Our expectation is that there will be no need to return the design to the front-end team because it failed to meet its targets or encountered congestion problems. That is the fundamental change we aim to bring to the transition between front-end and back-end chip development.

Modern SoCs typically combine proprietary logic with third-party IP, including processor cores, memory controllers, interface IP, and other reusable components. However, developers do not necessarily have access to the RTL of licensed IP blocks, and licensing agreements may restrict how such information can be used. This raises the question of how ACI can integrate third-party IP without access to its internal implementation.

According to Cognichip, this is not a problem. ACI does not need to examine proprietary RTL to integrate an existing IP block into a larger design. Such IPs provide relevant interface specifications, including pin connections, signals, and their characteristics. ACI can then proceed with necessary integration logic and connect the IP to other subsystems.

"Most people want to take […] third-party licensed IP and optimize the integration of the IP," claims Diamantidis. "We ourselves do not ingest the guts of the IPs, nor do we try to train on any kind of data related to the IPs."

The CPO of Cognichip stressed that ACI Enterprise protects customers' IP within the company's firewalled data centers and prevents it from entering third-party AI training pipelines. The platform provides customer-controlled access to sensitive information, multi-tenant isolation, and security controls validated through a SOC 2 Type II examination. However, these protections do not supersede the licensing restrictions imposed by third-party IP providers.

Cognichip's ACI technology could substantially improve chip development productivity by automating labor-intensive tasks such as architectural exploration, RTL development, verification, and PPA optimization.

The company's benchmark with a major chip designer suggests that the potential gains could be considerable, although the complexity of the project remains undisclosed. Such capabilities could be particularly valuable for startups and newcomers to the semiconductor industry, which tend to lack engineering resources and extensive IP portfolios of established chipmakers. By reducing the time, costs, and expertise required to develop custom silicon, ACI could lower the barriers to entry and enable smaller companies to pursue a custom silicon strategy that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive.

However, Cognichip has yet to demonstrate autonomous development of a complete, physically validated chip, let alone a sophisticated CPU or GPU. The company does not perform physical implementation, and its expectations of eliminating costly feedback loops depend on the accuracy of its PPA predictions. It also remains to be seen how effectively ACI can optimize complex SoCs that combine numerous proprietary and third-party IP blocks under common power, performance, and area constraints.

Ultimately, the Cognichip technology's value for leading-edge chip developers will depend not only on how quickly it can produce verified RTL, but also on how closely its predictions match the results of physical implementation and how much engineering work it can eliminate across the entire development cycle.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

#10473. A major change to the U.S. mortgage market could be coming. Here’s why homeowners should care

As President Donald Trump enters the lame-duck era of his presidency, questions remain about which of his various agenda items will actually get accomplished.

One of his long-standing goals has been to end the government conservatorship that mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have been subject to since the financial crisis of 2008. After failing to make much headway during his first term in office, Trump revived those intentions for his second term—but once again hasn’t made it much of a priority.

This past May, Trump posted on Truth Social that he was “working on taking these amazing companies public,” while adding that the U.S. government would retain its mortgage guarantees and oversight role for both government-sponsored entities. But only a matter of days later, when asked about an initial public offering for Fannie and Freddie, Trump said: “It’s not a rush.”

Meanwhile, Trump also sees the current government control of Fannie and Freddie as an opportunity to address housing affordability. On the eve of the midterm elections, he announced at a rally in Kansas that the entities would invest $4.3 billion in home loans in the state next year, which he promised would help 15,000 people achieve their American dream.

Removing Fannie and Freddie from conservatorship, experts have cautioned, could push up mortgage rates. And because Democrats regained control of Congress by campaigning on affordability, that may make them reluctant to entertain an end to this long-standing conservatorship now, when so many Americans are grappling with an affordability crisis. 

Further complicating matters is how, exactly, the Trump administration could go about ending the conservatorship—whether by an executive order or with support from Congress. Legal and political analysts are divided on whether that could happen or if Trump would need support from Congress, as Realtor.com reported.  

Frank Cassidy, the former federal housing commissioner in Trump’s second term, told the outlet that Trump can privatize Fannie and Freddie without Republican control of Congress, but noted that how they were structured post-conservatorship would matter. 

“It hasn’t been a priority yet,” Cassidy told Realtor.com. “It would need to be worked on very quickly because it will take some time.” 

A PUSH FROM WALL STREET

One person who’d very much like privatizing Fannie and Freddie to be a priority is hedge funder Bill Ackman. He says that removing these entities from conservatorship would be “helpful” for improving housing affordability because it would remove any political uncertainty from the mortgage market, particularly if Democrats were to use Fannie and Freddie in the future to “achieve political objectives.”

Of course, he has an incentive at stake: His firm, Pershing Square, is invested in both Fannie and Freddie. Though the companies were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010, they have traded in the over-the-counter market ever since.

Still, Ackman argues that Americans stand to benefit from ending the conservatorship. “This is a major point of economic policy where the president can have a hundreds of billion-dollar win for the American people,” he told CNBC, adding that it could be a “windfall” to the tune of $500 billion.

WEIGHING THE CONSEQUENCES

Such optimism for a widespread benefit to Americans counters what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressed on a 2Way podcast appearance last month. 

While Bessent said that the Trump administration will tackle the ownership structure of Fannie and Freddie in either 2027 or 2028, he said the “north star” guiding a decision will be whether ending the conservatorship can be accomplished without meaningfully increasing the spread between mortgage-backed securities and Treasury yields.

“It’s unclear why homeowners or mortgage holders would benefit from a change in the arrangement of the shareholder structure,” Bessent said.

What people on both sides of the political aisle can agree on is that a rush to end an 18-year arrangement would be most problematic. Still, the clock is ticking on Trump’s time in office to accomplish this goal, with less than 800 days remaining. 

And one person who could stand in the way is Rep. Maxine Waters, a Democrat from California, who is running to chair the House Financial Services Committee again after serving on it for more than a decade. 

As Realtor.com reported, Waters has historically opposed any efforts to rapidly end the conservatorship without comprehensive congressional oversight. “To address the affordable housing crisis, Congress must ensure that Fannie and Freddie meet their mission to provide liquidity, sustainability, and affordability to all housing markets in the U.S., and at all times,” Waters said at a hearing in April.

#10470. CEOs still think they can get away with affairs after #MeToo

Nearly a decade after the #MeToo movement burst into public consciousness, the upheaval at Nvidia may be a lesson in how little CEOs seem to have learned. 

Nvidia’s embattled CEO, Jensen Huang, has resigned following a New York Times report on Wednesday that revealed he had engaged in another extramarital relationship—this time involving a subordinate, the company’s vice president of healthcare and one of his 60 direct reports. The affair was a blatant violation of Nvidia’s code of conduct, which notes that employees should steer clear of situations that could create a conflict of interest, including “personal relationships.” The company also purports to “promptly investigate” reports of misconduct.

While this dalliance has fewer national security implications than his entanglement with an alleged Chinese spy, it does suggest that CEOs like Huang don’t expect to face consequences for getting involved with employees. 

Huang is in good company: Many employers have similar policies that forbid romantic relationships between managers and their direct reports, but that hasn’t stopped executives from crossing the line anyway. (Who could forget the viral video of the Astronomer CEO caught canoodling with his chief people officer at a Coldplay concert?)

In recent years, however, a number of executives have been forced to step down after pursuing inappropriate relationships, in addition to CEOs like Leslie Moonves (formerly head of CBS) being fired for sexual harassment. 

Back in 2019, McDonald’s then-CEO Steve Easterbrook was ousted over a relationship with a subordinate. Later he was sued by the company for concealing other relationships with employees and misleading investors. (He was eventually forced to pay back his $105 million severance package.)

There was Alan Shaw, former CEO of Norfolk Southern railroad, who was let go in 2024 over his relationship with the company’s chief legal officer. Last year, Nestlé SA CEO Laurent Freixe was given the boot after an internal investigation confirmed a relationship with a subordinate (which Freixe had initially denied). Kohl’s CEO Ashley Buchanan was also recently forced out when the board learned that he had given millions of dollars in business to a vendor he was dating without disclosing the relationship.

The fact that CEOs continue to pursue their subordinates, regardless of the consequences, may seem like a sign that the #MeToo movement is in the rearview. Perhaps some executives truly believe they are irreplaceable, or that there is now limited public pressure, years after #MeToo took hold. 

But Amy Nicole Baker, a professor at the University of New Haven who studies workplace romance, argues that not much has shifted after #MeToo, either in terms of CEO behavior or how companies tend to handle these situations. 

“The stock price goes down, at least in the short term,” she says, citing her research on how stock prices are impacted by sexual harassment allegations or affairs involving the CEO. “And usually CEOs are removed and replaced.”

Boards tend to have limited tolerance for the behavior, which they view as a sign of poor judgment. Indiscretions like an extramarital affair or otherwise inappropriate relationship can set off alarm bells or lead board members to wonder what else a CEO is hiding. “Boards look at CEO behavior as a signal for what could be going on in the internal management of the company,” Baker says.  

Still, it appears CEOs don’t necessarily feel constrained by those expectations, or the rules they impose on their employees—even when their own peers have been in the line of fire. 

“People show less restraint when they are in power, and they’re also more likely to perceive someone else sending them sexual signals when they’re actually not,” Baker says. “So the research on power can tell us a little bit about why this keeps happening.” 

People in positions of power tend to be more impulsive and comfortable with risk—something they are often rewarded for in a business context. Company culture can also reinforce that behavior, if it’s more informal and encourages people to push boundaries. “If you’re willing to break a rule in one way, it’s probably more acceptable to tacitly break a rule in a different way,” Baker says. 

The intense scrutiny of Huang’s misdeeds might discourage some CEOs from engaging in relationships with subordinates or other inappropriate behavior—but likely not for long. 

“In terms of the CEOs and their propensity to get involved in risky workplace relationships, that doesn’t seem to have changed,” Baker says. “More people are willing to say, ‘Yes, this happened to me. Yes, this is an issue. Yes, this is a problem.’ There’s certainly more recognition and awareness. But when it comes to people at this highest echelon, I’m not seeing a change in behavior.”

#10469. Why Your AI Agent Can't Read the Web (and How to Build a Fetch Layer That Can)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

This is the least glamorous part of building with LLMs and it's where a lot of agent projects quietly fall over. The model is rarely the problem. The fetch is. In this article we'll look at why live web retrieval has become so unreliable for AI tools, what the numbers say about the shift, and how to build a small, well-behaved fetch layer in Python that fails loudly instead of feeding your model garbage.

A few years ago, a plain requests.get() worked on most of the public web. That's no longer true, and the reason is simple: there are now more bots than people.

According to the 2025 Imperva Bad Bot Report, automated traffic made up 51% of all web traffic in 2024. That's the first time in a decade it has passed human activity. Bad bots alone (scrapers, credential stuffers, scalpers) went from 32% to 37% of traffic in a single year.

Source: Imperva Bad Bot Report 2024 and 2025

From a site owner's point of view, your polite research agent and a credential-stuffing botnet look much the same at the network edge. Both are non-browser clients making fast requests from data-center IP ranges. So the defaults have tightened. In July 2025 Cloudflare began blocking known AI crawlers by default for new customers, and bot management products now look at TLS fingerprints, header order, IP reputation and JavaScript execution, not just the User-Agent string.

It helps to understand the publisher's side of the deal, because it explains why your agent is being treated with suspicion.

Cloudflare splits AI crawling into three purposes: training (collecting data to train models), search (building an index for AI search answers) and user action (fetching a page because a person just asked a question). Training dominates.

Training crawls take content and send nothing back. Cloudflare measures this with a crawl-to-referral ratio: how many pages a platform crawls for every visitor it sends to the site. In its crawl-to-click gap analysis, the ratios for some AI platforms ran into the tens of thousands, compared with single digits for traditional search.

If you ran a publication and saw those numbers, you'd block too. The catch is that blocking is usually done by user agent or IP range, so it hits user-action fetches as well. Those are the ones that happen when a person asks your agent to read a specific article, and Cloudflare's 2025 Year in Review found they grew more than 15x during the year. Your agent is caught in a fight it didn't start.

The mix of crawlers also shifts quickly, which makes static allow and block lists fragile on both sides:

And restrictions keep piling up. The Consent in Crisis study audited 14,000 web domains and found that a large and fast-growing share of the sources behind the C4 training corpus now restrict AI crawlers, either through robots.txt or their terms of service.

Source: Longpre et al., Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024)

So that's the environment your agent fetches in. Here's how to build for it.

Before writing any retry logic, put names on your failures. "The request failed" is useless to both you and the model. In practice almost every failed fetch falls into one of four buckets:

Bucket 2 is the dangerous one, because a block page often comes back with a 200 OK. If you don't check, the model will happily summarise "Checking your browser before accessing..." as if it were the article.

Here's a compact fetch layer in Python using httpx and the standard library's robots.txt parser. It's around 100 lines and covers the four buckets above.

Use a descriptive user agent with a contact URL. It costs you nothing and site operators are far more likely to allow a client they can identify and reach. Then check robots.txt (standardised as RFC 9309) before every new host.

The lru_cache means you fetch robots.txt once per origin rather than once per page. In a long-running service you'll want a cache with a TTL instead, since robots.txt files do change.

This is the core of the layer. Instead of returning raw HTML, return a result that says which bucket you landed in.

The marker list is deliberately simple. It won't catch every interstitial, but it catches the common ones, and a false "blocked" is much cheaper than a confident summary of a CAPTCHA page. Log every blocked result with its first few hundred characters so you can grow the list from real data.

Retries should depend on the bucket. Throttled and broken responses get exponential backoff with jitter. Blocked and not-allowed responses get no retries at all.

Note the cap on wait. A site sending Retry-After: 3600 is telling you to go away for an hour. An interactive agent should report that to the user rather than block a request thread for that long.

The cheapest fetch is the one you don't make. Agents often re-read the same documentation page several times in one session. Store the ETag and Last-Modified headers and send them back as If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. A 304 Not Modified response costs the server almost nothing and lowers the odds of being rate limited.

Wire these into fetch() by passing headers=conditional_headers(url) to client.get(). On a 304, return the cached text. On a 200, call remember().

Finally, don't hide failures from the LLM. Give the tool output a structured shape so the model can reason about it:

(extract_main_text is whatever readability or boilerplate-removal step you already use. Libraries like trafilatura work well here.)

With this in place, the model's answer changes from a made-up summary to "I couldn't read that page because the site blocks automated access. Here's what I found from two other sources." That's a better product, and it builds trust with users.

Once you've done everything above, some legitimate user-action fetches will still fail. That's usually because the site blocks data-center IP ranges outright, not because of anything your agent did. Teams handle this in a few ways, roughly in order of preference:

The principle is the same in every case: the network path is a reliability decision, not a way around a site's wishes. Your robots.txt check and your honest user agent should stay in place whichever route the request takes.

Once your fetch layer returns structured results, observability is easy. Emit one event per fetch with the host, status bucket and latency, and watch these:

If you're prototyping agents with AI coding assistants, ask them to generate these metrics hooks from the start. They're easy to bolt on now and painful to add later. For a sense of how well current tools handle this kind of infrastructure code, Vibe Coder Journal publishes hands-on reviews and benchmarks of AI coding tools.

The web your agent reads in 2026 isn't the open, fetch-anything web many of us learned on. More than half the traffic is automated, publishers have good reasons to be wary of AI crawlers, and the defaults now lean toward blocking. You can't change that. You can make your agent a good citizen, though: one that identifies itself, respects the rules, backs off when asked, and tells the truth when it can't read something.

Most of the reliability gains come from the unglamorous parts: classifying failures, caching and passing honest errors to the model. Get those right and your agent will feel much more dependable, even on the days when half the web won't let it in.

It depends on the jurisdiction, the site's terms of service and what you do with the content. Respecting robots.txt and site terms is the baseline. For commercial products, get proper legal advice.

Many site owners expect it to, and RFC 9309 makes no exception for user-triggered fetches. The safest default is to obey it and tell the user when a page is disallowed.

Many bot-protection systems serve a challenge page with a 200 status. Check the body for challenge markers before passing it to the model, as in the looks_blocked() function above.

Only for pages that render their main content with JavaScript. Try a plain HTTP fetch first. Headless browsers are slower, cost more to run and are easier to fingerprint.

#10467. Kalshi will pay you $120,000 to play ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’

People are already calling out sick to play the feverishly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI. Companies like Logitech are even giving staff paid time off to partake. 

Now, thanks to prediction market Kalshi, folks won’t have to play hooky from their jobs to dive into the video game—the first installment in 13 years of Rockstar Games’ hit franchise that has earned the company billions worldwide. Instead, one person can make playing it their literal job.

Kalshi will pay a lucky gamer between $100,000 and $120,000 to play Grand Theft Auto VI’s story mode through to completion, starting right at midnight on launch day, November 19. The winning applicant will stream their digital criminal adventures on YouTube or Twitch as they explore the fictional U.S. state of Leonida as the Bonnie-and-Clyde main character couple, Jason and Lucia.

The ideal candidate is “an experienced gamer” and “streamer with your own channel,” the listing states, along with “18+ years of life IRL, 10+ years of sweaty gaming, 3+ years of streaming experience.” They’ll get an extra $15,000 upon completion of the project.

As Kalshi’s “researcher”—and yes, per the LinkedIn post, the company assures that this is a real job—the winning candidate will be tasked with exploring and studying Leonida’s in-game economy of robberies and heists, perfecting the “optimal moneymaking strategy” and building “a spreadsheet to prove it,” to the point where they’ll get “accused of ruining the game for everyone else.”

In addition to unpacking the way fictional money moves in Vice City, the researcher is apparently also tasked with monitoring the game’s effects on the actual economy—tracking, for example, “who called in ‘sick,’ how DoorDash carried the entire nation through launch week, and how much productivity America lost,” the listing states. 

Kalshi’s interest in the cultural and economic impacts of the game are well founded: The Wall Street Journal has warned of a “work blackout” upon its release, and one Spanish economist estimated the U.S. economy will lose $1 billion in productivity due to absenteeism.

And according to a poll released last month that surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults 18 or older who are employed full time and play video games regularly, 39% said they were planning to request time off in advance to play GTA VI, 36% said they’ll call in sick, and 32% said they’d “work” from home on release day. Many anticipate catching “GTA flu.”

Grand Theft Auto VI, which is being called “the biggest entertainment launch in history,” arrives Thursday, November 19, on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S consoles. Digital preorders have broken records, generating $1 billion from over 10 million units sold worldwide, according to estimates.

The researcher listing hasn’t even been up for 24 hours, and “over 100 people have clicked apply,” according to the LinkedIn post—something nobody needed Kalshi to predict.

Even open-source isn't safe from Nintendo's legal team

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nintendo has set its famously litigious sights on the open-source firmware that powers hardware modchips on Nintendo Switch. Earlier this week, GitHub posted a DCMA request from Nintendo of America confirming that an entire network of 144 total repositories, including the parent repository, was taken down. Mod chip firmware for hardware including SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly, and HWFLY was targeted.

Early original Nintendo Switch consoles shipped with an unpatchable hardware exploit found in the device's recovery mode, which has since been patched in later units such as the Switch Lite and Switch OLED (the modchip hack doesn't work on Switch 2). As such, running custom software on patched Switches requires hardware modification, soldering a microchip like a Picofly, HWFLY, or SX Core to your Switch's motherboard. These chips require firmware, specifically code that can perform the voltage glitching required during boot to hack the Switch.

Rather than playing whack-a-mole with vendors of off-the-shelf microcontrollers, Nintendo has instead issued a DCMA takedown notice to the entire family of GitHub repos hosting this firmware. "The reported repositories offer, link to, or otherwise provide access to mod chip firmware including but not limited to SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly, or HWFLY," the DCMA request from Nintendo reads. "The firmware allows Nintendo Switch modchips to illegally circumvent Nintendo’s TPMs in order to run illegal copies of Nintendo Switch games. Specifically, during operation, the mod chip firmware at the reported repositories circumvents the technological protection measures put in place on the Nintendo Switch console by bypassing the boot sequence.

Nintendo went on to state that because these repositories are designed "primarily" to unlawfully circumvent technological measures controlling access to work protected under the DCMA, distributing mod chip firmware "constitutes unlawful trafficking in technology that is 'primarily designed or produced for the purpose of circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access' to copyrighted works." In support of this argument, Nintendo cited criminal proceedings brought by the US Department of Justice against Team-Xecuter, a maker and seller of SX Pro, SX Core, and SX Lite modchips.

While these modchips can be (and are) used for game piracy, they unlock a host of features including running homebrew and custom applications, emulation, alternative operating systems, and more. They also enable game modding, custom themes, and even Switch overclocking. Naturally, Nintendo has chosen to focus on their utility in accessing pirated games and bypassing DRM.

Because much of this hardware and firmware is already out in the wild, the move won't have any impact on existing Switch owners who have a modchip installed. However, this will prevent firmware updates to existing modchips, as well as firmware flashing and reflashing. Naturally, it will also prevent future potential hardware modders from hacking their Switch in the same way.

Nintendo is famous for its fervent prosecution of copyright law, but developments in AI are turning this into a drastically more complicated battle. Nintendo's Zelda remake was dumped online on the same day it launched on Switch 2, while earlier this year one developer used AI to bring the original Nintendo 64 version to iOS. In July, Mario Kart Wii was recompiled for PC in 4K with over 200 tracks.

#10459. How to Use CSS Attribute Selectors to Build More Flexible User Interfaces

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When developing a website, developers often rely on CSS classes to style buttons, forms, navigation elements, and other interface components. This approach works well, but some situations require styles to depend on an element's HTML attributes rather than additional class names.

CSS attribute selectors provide a practical solution. They allow developers to target elements based on whether an attribute exists, what value it contains, or whether its value matches a particular pattern. Used carefully, they can simplify styling and make reusable components easier to maintain.

An attribute selector targets an HTML element using square brackets. For example, a developer can select every input field that has a required attribute:

This rule applies to inputs with the required attribute, regardless of their input type.

Developers can also target a specific attribute value:

This is useful when different input types need different visual treatments without introducing additional classes into the HTML.

Forms are a practical place to apply attribute selectors because HTML already provides attributes that describe how individual fields behave.

Consider a registration form containing email, password, and telephone fields. Each input can be styled according to its purpose:

The CSS can target these fields independently:

This approach keeps the markup descriptive while allowing the stylesheet to respond to the attributes already present in the document.

One important distinction is that required indicates a validation requirement, while :invalid represents an input's current validity state. These should not be treated as interchangeable.

CSS provides several matching operators that help developers target more specific attribute values.

These operators can be useful when working with links, downloadable files, language attributes, and reusable components.

For example, a website might want to distinguish PDF downloads from ordinary navigation links:

This adds a small visual indicator to links whose URLs end in .pdf.

Attribute selectors can also help identify links with different destinations or behaviors.

For example, external links that use HTTPS can receive a subtle visual indicator:

However, matching an HTTPS URL does not necessarily prove that a link points to an external website. Internal links can also use HTTPS, so developers should consider the actual navigation requirements before applying special styling.

For more examples of selector combinations and matching rules, SitePoint's guide to CSS Attribute Selectors provides a useful reference.

Although attribute selectors are flexible, they should not replace every class-based styling decision.

A selector such as [class*="button"] can match unintended elements if their class names happen to contain the same text. Similarly, broad attribute rules may affect components that were not originally intended to receive those styles.

For predictable results, use exact attribute matching whenever possible and prefer descriptive classes for major component styling.

Developers should also remember that CSS selectors only control presentation. They do not replace JavaScript validation, server-side security checks, or proper HTML semantics.

The MDN documentation on attribute selectors provides further details about selector syntax, matching behavior, and supported operators.

Before adding attribute selectors to a large stylesheet, inspect the affected elements using browser developer tools.

Check whether the selector matches the intended elements.

Test fields with different attribute values.

Verify disabled, required, and invalid form states.

Check navigation links and downloadable files.

Test the layout on mobile and desktop screens.

Review whether existing component styles are being unintentionally overridden.

This process helps identify unexpected matches before they affect the production interface.

CSS attribute selectors give developers another way to create flexible and maintainable interfaces without adding unnecessary classes to every HTML element.

They are particularly useful for form styling, link identification, and components that already contain meaningful HTML attributes. By choosing precise selectors, understanding matching operators, and testing changes before deployment, developers can use this feature to write cleaner CSS while keeping their markup descriptive and organized.

#10454. Hunter is killing Google Home, Alexa controls for its smart ceiling fans

Hunter, a major brand for ceiling fans in the US, is pulling the plug on its Google Home and Amazon Alexa bridge for controlling “HunterSMART” models in just a few weeks.

Effective January 1, 2027, Hunter will pull support for the cloud-reliant “HunterSMART” connection used for Google Home and Amazon Alexa controls. Hunter’s app and the included remote will continue to work, but connections to smart home ecosystems will not.

Beginning January 1, 2027, the legacy cloud-to-cloud connections used for app linking between the HunterSMART™ mobile apps and Google Home and/or Amazon Alexa will no longer be supported.

After this date, Google home and Alexa functionality that relies on this legacy cloud connection will no longer work for HunterSMART fans, including voice commands, scenes, and automations.

This bridge is going away in favor of a Matter connection, with Hunter having been upgrading select models to be Matter-compatible over the past year. But this is only available to “eligible” models, not everyone who was already using Hunter’s existing bridge. A list of compatible models is available on Hunter’s website, with firmware updates rolling out via the HunterSMART app.

Some models, such as the one I reviewed a few years ago, require updated hardware. Besides that, the one I have can’t even be re-connected to Wi-Fi to check for an update as Hunter’s Android app consistently crashes during the setup process.

Once the fan has been updated, it won’t be available via the existing link and will instead require re-pairing via your smart home app of choice, whether that’s Google Home or another.

…Hunter is transitioning eligible HunterSMART™ products to Matter, an industry standard designed to support broader smart-home compatibility.

If your fan is eligible for Matter-compatibility, you will be able to continue using all smart functionality within the Google Home and/or Alexa ecosystems after completing the applicable Matter migration & setup.

Once your HunterSMART fan is Matter-enabled, connecting your fan to Google and Alexa will work differently than it does today. Instead of linking your HunterSMART account to Google Home or Alexa, you will need to setup your Matter-enabled fan directly into these compatible ecosystems using the Matter setup available via the Google Home and/or Alexa apps. Matter-enabled devices do not use the legacy cloud linking service for smart controls that is being discontinued.

How can I migrate my HunterSMART fan to Matter?

Depending on your fan model and hardware configuration, a firmware update or updated hardware components may be required for Matter compatibility. Available Matter upgrade options and instructions will vary by product. You can visit our HunterSMART™ Matter resource page for the latest information about Matter compatibility, available upgrade options, and next steps.

#10452. Googlebook apps built by Googlers add macOS-like status bar shortcuts, keyboard commands

Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the company’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.

In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.

“BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more. It’s full of glancable information such as weather conditions, battery charging speeds, and more, but also includes useful tools such as being able to access a clipboard history, set a timer, and more. The app requires permissions including accessibility overlays, but it works like a charm.

I had no idea the status bar on Googlebook could even be used like this, and it really makes that space a lot more useful. Of course, you have to draw a comparison here to macOS, which also uses this space for app shortcuts and tools, though BentoBox offers a different type of customization.

BentoBox is available for download via Google Play for free.

The other Mac-like app here is “Booklight,” a launcher that’s basically Apple’s Spotlight, just for Googlebook. It has a transparent design and lets you search “apps, settings, and the web.”

Technically, Googlebook already can do this in its built-in search bar (in the app drawer), but Booklight has more customization and functionality, including being able to write out shorthand commands all in one sentence with the app then completing the command in the appropriate apps, as well as having a clearer UI for experiences such as typing in quick math equations. It’s also good at finding symbols (so you don’t have to remember the U+ codes that carried over from ChromeOS). Not one I found myself wanting to use, but the potential is there.

Both BentoBox and Booklight were developed by Alexander Kuscher, VP over Laptops & Tablets at Google.

The other app highlighted in Google’s thread was Wayfinder, a file manager app described as a “desktop-grade file manager.” The big bonus here is network file access for NAS boxes and other uses, but the app also just has a more advanced UX compared to Googlebook’s built-in Files app.

Googlebook’s app gap is a real problem at launch, but these apps do show there’s a lot of potential in the platform, it’s just a matter of getting developers on board – which itself will require Google and its partners to actually sell some of these laptops… classic chicken-and-egg situation.

#10451. How to Get a YouTube API Key and Use the Data API (2026)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

You need a YouTube API key the moment your app has to read anything from YouTube: a video's length, its view count, a channel's latest uploads. Getting one takes about five minutes. Using it well takes a little longer, because YouTube changed how its quota works in June 2026, and plenty of guides still describe the old rules.

In this guide we'll get a key, lock it down and test it. Then we'll use it from Node.js for three real jobs: adding up the length of a playlist, listing a channel's videos without spending a search, and estimating what a video earned. Along the way we'll cover what the YouTube API costs (nothing), how the 2026 quota works, and the errors you're most likely to hit.

A YouTube API key identifies your project to the YouTube Data API v3. With just a key, you can read public data:

A key isn't enough for anything that touches someone's account. Uploading videos, editing playlists or reading private data needs OAuth 2.0, where the user signs in and grants your app access.

You'll need a Google account. The YouTube Data API is free, so there's nothing to pay for.

The restrictions matter more than they look. A key is just a string in a URL, and anyone who copies an unrestricted one can spend your daily quota for you. With an API restriction, the key is useless for other Google APIs. With an application restriction, it only works from your server or your site. Changes to restrictions can take up to five minutes to apply, so don't panic if a request fails straight after you save.

Before writing any code, check the key with a single request. This one asks for the first video ever uploaded to YouTube, and uses the fields parameter to trim the response down to four values:

That request cost 1 unit of your daily quota, which brings us to the question everyone asks.

Yes. There's no charge per request and no paid plan. Instead you get a daily quota, and since June 1, 2026 it's split into separate buckets:

Google's quota calculator lists the cost of every method. Quotas reset at midnight Pacific Time. Every request costs at least 1 unit, including requests that fail, so a retry loop around a broken call can use up a day's quota on its own.

If you've read older guides, search is the big change. A search used to cost 100 units out of the same 10,000, so 100 searches emptied your whole day. Uploads were worse still, at about 1,600 units each until December 2025. Now both have their own buckets, and the 10,000 units are left for everything else.

To give you a feel for what 10,000 units buys, here's what each example in this guide costs:

You can't pay for more. To go above the defaults, fill in the YouTube API Services Audit and Quota Extension Form, which is linked from Google's page on quota and compliance audits. YouTube first audits your project to check it follows the YouTube API Services Terms of Service, then someone from the API team gets back to you. Google doesn't give a timeline, so apply well before you need the extra quota.

Most projects never need to. The rest of this guide is about getting a lot done with very few units.

The examples need Node.js 20.6 or later, for the built-in fetch and the --env-file flag. There are no packages to install. Make a folder with a .env file in it:

Every example imports one small helper. It builds the URL, adds your key and turns API errors into readable messages:

Run any example with node --env-file=.env followed by the file name.

YouTube doesn't tell you how long a playlist is. To work it out, you need two methods:

Durations come back in ISO 8601 format. PT15M33S is 15 minutes 33 seconds, PT1H2M3S adds an hour, and a stream longer than a day looks like P1DT2H3M4S. The toSeconds() function below handles all three.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Full Courses in One Video playlist:

That's 184 hours of courses for 4 units of quota. Private and deleted videos still show up in a playlist's items, but videos.list doesn't return them, which is why the script prints "52 of 52 videos available". On a playlist with removed videos, the two numbers will differ.

This is the core of the free YouTube playlist length calculator I built on createthat.ai. The live version adds a target time box that works out the speed you need to finish by a deadline, and it accepts channel, video and Shorts links as well as playlists.

The obvious way to find a channel's videos is to search for them. Don't: search is now capped at 100 calls a day, and it isn't built to list everything a channel has posted. Every channel has an uploads playlist instead, and you can reach it in two cheap calls:

Two units, and none of your 100 daily searches. To get every upload rather than the newest five, page through the playlist with the same pageToken loop as Example 1.

videos.list with part=statistics returns a video's view, like and comment counts. Dislike counts have been private since December 2021 and favoriteCount is always 0, so don't build anything on those. The script also copes with a missing like or comment count, which you'll see on some videos.

This time the fields parameter trims the response to the values we use. That makes the response smaller, but it doesn't change the cost: the call is 1 unit either way.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Learn Python full course, one of the most-watched videos in that playlist:

Treat the last line as a rough range, not an answer. The Data API doesn't share anyone's revenue, so any estimate is views multiplied by an RPM: what a creator keeps per 1,000 views. RPM moves a lot with the topic and where the viewers live, and the estimate assumes the video shows ads, which not every channel does.

And sometimes you don't need an API at all. When I built a font tester, I needed a list of Google Fonts. The Google Fonts Developer API would have meant a key and a call on every visit, for a list that barely changes. Instead I generated a file of the 500 most popular fonts once, from Google's public font metadata, and the page loads it like any other file. No key, no quota and nothing to fail.

When a call fails, the response's error.message and error.details[0].reason tell you why. These are the ones you'll see most:

For the invalid key error, the full response looks like this:

Yes. Creating a key and calling the YouTube Data API costs nothing. You're limited by the daily quota instead, and there's no paid tier: more quota comes through an audit.

In the Google Cloud console, select your project and go to APIs & Services > Credentials. Your keys are listed under API keys, with a Show key option next to each one.

It works, but anyone can read the key from your page. If you do it, restrict the key to your website and to the YouTube Data API v3. A small server route that calls the API for you is safer, and it gives you somewhere to cache results.

By default, 100 searches, 100 uploads and 10,000 units for everything else. Most reads cost 1 unit and videos.list takes 50 IDs per call, so that's enough for the details of up to 500,000 videos a day.

Getting a YouTube API key is the easy part: one project, one API to enable, one key and two restrictions. The 2026 quota is generous if you work with it:

All three examples together cost 7 units, out of 10,000. From here, try commentThreads.list to pull a video's comments 100 at a time, or extend Example 2 to page through a channel's entire upload history and add it all up with the code from Example 1.

#10449. Fitbit Sense & Versa losing 3rd-party watch faces this month, existing downloads remain

Google announced today that Fitbit Sense and Versa smartwatches will soon lose the ability to “install or update third-party apps and clocks.”

This change to the Fitbit App Gallery applies to the Versa, Versa 2, Versa 3, Versa 4, Sense, and Sense 2.

Existing “third-party apps or clock faces installed on your Fitbit device” will remain available, but you can no longer download new ones (or update them) starting November 28. As such, “if you choose to delete an app or clock face, or factory reset your device, you will no longer be able to re-install it.”

Instead, the Fitbit App Gallery will “exclusively feature apps and clock faces created by Fitbit and Google.”

The November 28 deadline also applies to third-party developers. Google will “no longer support uploading new apps and clock faces or updating existing ones.”

Google winding down Fitbit OS for smartwatches is not particularly surprising as the company has been all-in on Wear OS and the Pixel Watch. That said, the Sense 2 and Versa 4 should probably no longer be on sale.

The King 95 3D is a solid, premium-class mid-tower with three tempered-glass panels for panoramic views inside. The seven included Link fans on the Pro version deliver enough airflow and RGB bling, but can get noisy at full speed. For $119 or $199 for the Pro, it’s an excellent update from the original King 95.

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

PC case, cooling, and PSU maker Montech is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year and has released a new flagship ATX chassis, the King 95 3D and 3D Pro. Like the previous King 95, the 3D version keeps the signature 15-degree curved-glass panoramic front panel and adds a top glass panel, giving you a third window and a unique aesthetic for viewing your build. An integrated, contoured ARGB strip follows the chassis's smooth lines, making it look every bit the king of the castle.

Inside, the large mid-tower chassis supports multiple radiators (though only one 360mm), large graphics cards (plus integrated adjustable GPU support), CPU air coolers, and spots for 2.5- and 3.5-inch drives. However, it doesn't support E-ATX motherboards. The King 95 3D supports rear-connect motherboards and has ample room for cable routing and management. The front aluminum panel IO runs vertically, as with previous King cases, and includes a fast USB 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C port. Overall, it has everything you want in a premium chassis. The uncommon three-panel view into your PC is a great way to show off your rig.

The King 95 3D is available for an inexpensive (at least for curved glass) $119.90 if you want to select your own fans. The 3D Pro includes seven pre-installed LINK Fan INF 120 fans for builders who want a more coordinated look out of the box, plus it includes the Lumi hub (a dedicated fan controller), for $199.90. We have the 3D Pro version in our lab and ran the case through thermal and noise testing in its out-of-the-box configuration to show how it performs compared to others. Will it make our best PC cases list? It has a chance. But before we get into the details, here are the case's specifications from Montech.

21 x 21 x 18.8 x 11.8-inches (534 x 480 x 300mm)

Top - 3x120Front - N/ABottom - 3x120mmSide: - 2x120mmRear - 2x120mm

(5) Link Fan INF 120 (Reverse blades, side/bottom)(2) Link Fan INF 120 (rear)

Front - N/ATop - 120/240/360mmSide - 120/240mmRear - 120mm

Great internal views, 7x pre-installed fans (Pro version), integrated GPU support, adjustable angle bottom fans

King 95 3D - $119.90 (w/o fans)King 95 3D Pro - $199.90 (w/7 pre-installed fans)

From the outside, the King 95 3D Pro looks the part of its royal name. That signature curve and three panes of glass offer a panoramic view inside your case like few others, letting you show off your PC from even more angles. It also features a frosted, continuous LED strip running along the tiered top, right side, and bottom, adding some tasteful bling to the chassis. If you get the Pro version with the seven fans, it’s an RGB light show inside which could be polarizing. I do wish there were an option for preinstalled non-RGB fans, since the seven included ones and the infinity mirror styling may not be for everyone. Still, the curved front corner and clean lines really cement the King 95 3D as one of the better-looking panoramic cases on the market.

Up front, the removable curved glass corner with a smoked tint sets it apart from most others. On the right, the front IO panel runs vertically, with the power button on top and the LED on/off button below. It has three USB ports: one 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C and two USB 3.2 Gen1 (5 Gbps) Type-A ports. Finally, it has a 3.5mm audio jack. That continuous 118-LED strip is visible from the front, running along the top, down the right edge, and along the bottom edge. I’m not a fan of a lot of RGB, but this implementation is tasteful. You can control this lighting through the motherboard software or Montech's Lumi software, which lets you fully customize the fans and RGB strip.

The main window panel also uses a smoke-colored tint, with Montech branding in the upper-right corner, and it's secured to the frame by two captive thumbscrews on the back. To remove it, loosen the thumbscrews, slide the panel back, pull from the top, then lift it out of the slots. Easy. I have to say, the biggest problem with all this glass is keeping it pristine and fingerprint-free.The other (metal) side panel, behind the motherboard, slots into the frame and is secured the same way. It has filtered venting along the top and side for the fans/radiator locations, plus another area for airflow near the power supply and drive mounting locations. In the middle is a gold placard with Montech King 95 3D 10th anniversary badging. Note: The dust filters on this panel aren't removable, so you’ll need to remove the whole panel to clean things up.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

At the top, we get a better look at the third windowed panel, letting observers peer into the case from a different angle rather than straight on or from the front. We can also see the tiered top and part of the long RGB strip. Taking this panel off isn’t as simple as the rest. Yes, it’s also secured by two captive thumbscrews on the back, but to remove it, you’ll need to open the main window panel to expose a retaining screw, remove it, then loosen the back thumbscrews and slide it to the rear. After you remove the top glass, you can remove the upper and side retaining screws to take it out. When building, I didn’t find this necessary, but it’s good to know you can take it apart if needed.

Looking at the case from behind, one of the first things I noticed was the vertical PSU mounting location on the left. This space supports up to 220mm power supplies, which is all but the largest on the market. On the right, we see space for two 120mm fans, the motherboard I/O, and seven horizontal expansion slots. Unfortunately, Montech says the King 95 3D does not support vertical GPUs.

Underneath the case, there isn’t a lot going on. We get a better look at the four short rubber-bottom ‘feet’ and the removable dust filter. Montech put on its thinking cap and designed the dust filter to slide out from the front, so chances are you won’t have to move your heavy case to clean it.

Inside, the case uses a dual-chamber design, with the power supply and all wires hidden behind the motherboard tray. At the bottom, we see three Link Fan INF 120s (reverse blade) along with the mirror finish. The magnetically linked, daisy-chainable fans run up to 2,300 RPM (2,200 RPM on the reverse blade), pushing between 65-67 CFM with a maximum rating of 32dBA (29 dBA on the standard blade). A single Link Fan INF 120 costs $19.90, while a 3-pack (with Lumi Hub) is $64.90. If you do the math for seven fans and the Lumi Hub, it’s cheaper to buy them with the case rather than separately.

When powered on, the mirrored sides become an infinity panel, and with all seven matching, it creates a consistent view across the build. The bottom fan bracket is adjustable, with three positions (8 degrees). We left it down during testing, but with it up, you can focus more air towards the GPU and show off whatever fans you put in the space.

The motherboard tray has plenty of cutouts to access the back of the motherboard for easy installation/removal of air coolers or AIO/custom water-cooling blocks. The case also supports rear-connect ecosystems, including Asus BTF, Gigabyte Stealth, and MSI Project Zero boards. Grommets surround the motherboard tray and are in ideal locations, but like most, they pull out easily when you try to route cables, especially those with larger connectors. I wish all case vendors would secure these better, since they're a pain to reinstall, especially when the case is full of cables.Up top, we can see the huge gap above the motherboard tray for more fans and radiators. The case cooled just fine with the seven included fans and our air cooler, though GPU temps ran a bit warmer in our noise-normalized testing. That top gap is begging to be filled with fans, even if only for aesthetics. If you plan to use an AIO cooler, this isn’t a problem, since the radiator/fans will fill the space.

From the front, you can see the two Link INF 120mm fans and, at the bottom, the tool-less, adjustable GPU support strut. The back has space to mount two 120mm fans or one 120mm radiator. You can also see the seven horizontal expansion slots held in by thumbnail screws.

Inside, the top of the case above the motherboard space fits up to three 120mm fans or a 360mm radiator. The space is offset back from the motherboard tray, which is a boon for cable management. Normally, there’s barely any room to route the EPS cables, but here there's plenty. Just note that if your build uses air cooling, you will need to fill that area with fans to make it look good. Otherwise, it’s just a blank open space above the motherboard.

On the rear side of the chassis, we get a good look at the space behind the motherboard tray and the fan baffles. There’s plenty of room to route cables, and Montech has multiple pre-installed Velcro straps for cable routing. Even with the power supply installed, there’s plenty of room underneath it to stash excess cables.

At the bottom, we see a simple ARGB hub that consolidates the three different ARGB cables from the fans into one header to control all of them. Montech also includes a magnetic Lumi fan/RGB hub (which supports up to 13 Link Fans total) with both the Pro and non-Pro variants. Oddly, it comes loose/uninstalled on the Pro, but installed on the non-Pro. The box in the lower-right holds one 3.5-inch HDD and a single 2.5-inch drive. The second 2.5-inch drive mounts in the other location at the bottom left, next to the side fans.

We do like the look of the King 95 3D Pro case in black, and I bet it looks great in white with an all-white build too. The curved glass and 3-panel panoramic interior views are great for anyone who’d like to show off their now-ridiculously expensive parts. The included Link Fan INF 120 fans work well and run relatively quietly. If there’s an aesthetic drawback, it's that I’m not a huge fan of all the RGB and infinity mirrors on the pre-installed fans. It’s a lot, and it makes me yearn for an option with preinstalled fans and no RGB. Of course, you can turn them off in the software, or buy the non-Pro and choose whichever fans fit your build.

New leaks reveal the camera specs for Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series which includes three lenses across the lineup, but not the upgrades you want, nor what Ultra owners might expect.

SammyGuru reports that Samsung is “evaluating” camera setups for the Galaxy S27, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra, and it looks like a mixed bag across the board.

The base Galaxy S27 and S27+ are looking very familiar, with identical main camera sensors to last year, and the same ultrawide sensor that’s been in use since the Galaxy S23 series. The telephoto and selfie sensors are looking at new hardware, but without any major spec upgrades.

Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, meanwhile, have a new 200MP main camera on deck, a 50MP ultrawide shooter, and a mere 12MP telephoto. The Ultra might get 5x compared to the Pro’s 3x optical zoom, but with a secondary telephoto lens going missing, existing users of the lineup are sure to be disappointed.

Notably, SammyGuru’s article mentions the Pro as using “the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s 3x sensor,” but shows the 12MP Samsung S5K3LD in that place instead. We’re assuming that’s a typo seeing as the post mentions the Pro as using the Samsung S5KJN3 or the Sony IMX855 earlier on, but regardless, the Pro only gets 3x optical zoom to the Ultra’s 5x.

Some of these specs have been mentioned by other sources such as GalaxyClub and leaker Ice Universe, but this is the most complete picture of the S27’s camera plans we’ve seen to date.

Personally, I’m very “whelmed” on this one. As RAMageddon rages on and Samsung hunts for new ways to balance specs vs price, cameras are a place that’s obviously going to be cut, but competitors are already running laps around Samsung on the hardware front. Cutting lenses and skimping out on upgrades (again) doesn’t help matters.
